title: Akai is embracing vibe-coded mods with an open-source MPC
abstract: Gadgets AI Entertainment Akai is embracing vibe-coded mods with an open-source MPC The MPC Sample Key will be an open-source 37-key take on its budget-friendly MPC Sample. The MPC Sample Key will be an open-source 37-key take on its budget-friendly MPC Sample. by Terrence O'Brien Oct 28, 2026, 9:34 PM UTC The MPC Sample Key looks like the MPC Sample just with keys instead of pads. Image: Akai Part Of All the latest in AI ‘music’ see all updates Terrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths. The MPC Sample Key isn’t even formally announced yet, but Akai is already showing off what the modding community is cooking up through vibe coding. Akai has decided to embrace the explosion of hackers and custom firmware developers by giving them early access to the device, which will have open-source firmware. It will likely run some version of the same software found on the MPC Sample , but with tweaks to accommodate the traditional keyboard, pitch, and mod wheels. Unlike the higher-end MPC Key 37, however, the Sample Key doesn’t have pads. Instead, you play back samples with the keys. In the short Instagram Reels posted last night and today, Akai shows a number of vibe-coded mods that add synths, including Native Instruments Massive, to the device, as well as virtual analog and FM synths. One is even shown running a completely custom OS, with “several different synths in it.” According to the clips , the same “community” features will come to the regular MPC Sample, which is also shown running a few vibe-coded synths built by Claude. That could mean Akai plans to open-source the entire MPC Sample platform. CEO Jack O’Donnell told The Verge that inMusic brands, especially Akai, would be looking to embrace the modding community by seeding early devices to developers. These efforts will also include open-sourcing some software and providing an SDK. title: Google launches Gemini 4 Carbon with a ‘significant leap’ in cybersecurity
abstract: Tech AI News Google launches Gemini 4 Carbon with a ‘significant leap’ in cybersecurity Gemini 4 Carbon is outperforming the top models from OpenAI and Anthropic on some benchmarks. Gemini 4 Carbon is outperforming the top models from OpenAI and Anthropic on some benchmarks. by Emma Roth Oct 28, 2026, 8:03 PM UTC Image: The Verge Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Google has released its latest frontier model, Gemini 4 Carbon, offering “significant gains” in coding, agentic tasks, and cybersecurity. In an announcement on Wednesday , Google highlights Carbon’s top spot on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (v5.0) benchmark, with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra trailing behind. The new Gemini 4 Carbon model offers improvements over Argon, which Google released earlier this month. It’s currently only available to a select group of cybersecurity defense companies, but it will eventually expand to other partners in its Fairwind Program . Carbon sits ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. Image: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index The company says Carbon reflects the “pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward,” coming with a “significant leap” in cyberdefense that makes it better at finding vulnerabilities and generating secure code. Carbon currently holds the number one spot on SEC-bench Pro , a benchmark that measures an AI model’s ability to discover real-world bugs, and ExploitGym , which measures how a model can turn a vulnerability into exploits. Gemini 4 Carbon also beat GPT-6 Astra on the SEC-bench Pro cybersecurity benchmark. Image: Google Google says Gemini 4 Carbon is built for completing longer tasks, adding that its internal teams have seen it “run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks.” It’s also better at avoiding shortcuts, resisting prompt injection attacks, and collaborating with users, according to Google. Carbon is supposed to offer more “transparency and honesty” as well, by cutting “unsupported claims” by two times when compared to Argon. It will launch at the same competitive introductory price as Argon, at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. title: Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software
abstract: Back to Articles Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software Enterprise Article Published October 29, 2026 Upvote 10 +4 Kate Soule katesoule Follow ibm-granite Luis A Lastras GrizleeBer Follow ibm-granite Subhajit Chaudhury subhajit1412 Follow ibm-granite Abraham Daniels abedaniels Follow ibm-granite Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1 , showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint. Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood. Updated Granite Speech ASR model — multilingual speech-to-text across 10 languages with native punctuation and capitalization, so transcripts are ready for downstream models without a formatting pass. Updated Decision adapter in granitelib-core — featuring improved overall performance on the Jev Decision Index test set. While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy. This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon. Until then, test out our latest models , and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

title: Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready
abstract: Back to Articles Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready Published October 29, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 10 +4 Avijit Ghosh evijit Follow hfpolicy Sayeed Choudhury sayeedmd Follow CMU-OSPO Greg Tananbaum gtananbaum Follow ORCA-Open Emma Scharfmann EmmaScharfmann Follow hugging-science Georgia Channing cgeorgiaw Follow hugging-science Eunice Mercado-Lara EuniceML Follow ORCA-Open Irene Solaiman irenesolaiman Follow hfpolicy An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon. Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar , an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University , opens on November 2. See How to Participate below. The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University , Purdue University , Georgia Institute of Technology , Arizona State University , and The George Washington University , all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute ; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA) , through its Fostering Innovation Network , as the community partner. Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org . Making publicly funded science more usable The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development , and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data. But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines. Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI . The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release. The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains , including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models. The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025 , with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader. Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data . When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets . Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X . By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon. This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories. Open Science Challenges Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse. A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit? To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals: Demonstrate scientific reuse. Produce concrete examples of researchers and developers building on publicly funded scientific artifacts, including applications that combine resources across institutions or disciplines. Learn what makes reuse possible. Identify technical barriers, documentation gaps, interoperability challenges, and successful practices that can inform future research infrastructure, funding decisions, and public policy. The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful. The first challenge: Climate Risk Intelligence Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026 The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University , teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios. Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning.

Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms
abstract:
Back to Articles Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms Published October 29, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 6 Mattt mattt Follow Language models can do a lot.
They write, summarize, translate, and call tools.
But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do. Say a customer calls your support line.
First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition).
Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision).
You could hand both to a language model,
but there are models built for each that are
better, faster, and less expensive. In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap ,
we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases,
we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions:
familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model. Today we're announcing two packages: AnySpeechRecognizer implements Apple's new speech-to-text API with a choice of recognition engine,
including NVIDIA's Parakeet and Alibaba's Qwen3-ASR running locally on Core ML,
and adds speaker diarization to track who speaks when. AnyDecisionModel answers yes-or-no, multiple-choice, and rating-scale questions
with typed results and probabilities.
It derives each answer from the model's probabilities
instead of generating text,
using a model on your device with MLX, Core AI, or llama.cpp,
or a decision model from Jev or Ollama. Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub
and run them on device. AnySpeechRecognizer Computers have been transcribing speech for decades,
and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it.
Apple platforms already have an API for it.
macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer ,
Apple's new speech-to-text API.
You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer,
give it a file or a stream of audio buffers,
and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models,
so your app decides when downloads happen. It's a well-designed API,
but the only engine behind it is Apple's.
AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine: - import Speech + import AnySpeechRecognizer The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer , SpeechTranscriber , DictationTranscriber , SpeechDetector , and AssetInventory ,
with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine.
If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough.
To use Parakeet instead,
change only how you create the transcriber: let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber ( model: ParakeetSpeechModel (variant: .v3), transcriptionOptions: [], reportingOptions: [.volatileResults], attributeOptions: [.audioTimeRange]
) The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer,
and reading results stay the same.
The README has a complete example
and lists the differences from Apple's framework. Meet the models Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 .
It's a polyglot:
it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing,
so you don't pass a locale. Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3 .
It was more accurate in most of our measurements. Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet . All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime,
which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing,
and word confidence. Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model,
in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes.
It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects,
including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover.
It detects the language automatically, or you can set one: let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber ( model: QwenSpeechModel (variant: .large, language: Locale . Language (identifier: "yue" )), transcriptionOptions: [], reportingOptions: [], attributeOptions: []
) Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds,
without volatile results, word timing, or confidence.
It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet,
so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input. To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration
and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session.
The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started. Core ML models on the Hub To run these models in apps,
we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub: Model Core ML conversion Original checkpoint License Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 mattt/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3-coreml nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3 CC BY 4.0 Parakeet Ultra mattt/parakeet-ultra-coreml moondream/parakeet-ultra CC BY 4.0 Parakeet Unified EN 0.6B mattt/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b-coreml nvidia/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b NVIDIA Open Model License Qwen3-ASR 0.6B mattt/qwen3-asr-0.6b-coreml Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-0.6B-hf Apache 2.0 Qwen3-ASR 1.7B mattt/qwen3-asr-1.7b-coreml Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-1.7B-hf Apache 2.0 Streaming Sortformer 4spk v2 mattt/diar-streaming-sortformer-4spk-v2-coreml nvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2 CC BY 4.0 Streaming Sortformer 4spk v2.1 mattt/diar-streaming-sortformer-4spk-v2.1-coreml nvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2.1 NVIDIA Open Model License Each repository records its source checkpoint
and a checksum for every file,
and the package pins it to a fixed revision.
The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input,
which cuts live analysis time by about a third
at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate.
The repository also has the conversion workflows,
most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts,
and checks each conversion against the original model. Downloads happen only when your app asks for them:
about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder,
0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer.
Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache,
so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools. Speaker diarization When you transcribe a conversation,
you often want to know who said what.
That's speaker diarization,
and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it,
so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber,
on the same timeline: let diarizer = SpeakerDiarizer (model: SortformerDiarizationModel ()) if let request = try await AssetInventory .assetInstallationRequest( supporting: [transcriber, diarizer]
) { try await request.downloadAndInstall()
} let analyzer = SpeechAnalyzer (modules: [transcriber, diarizer]) The diarizer tracks up to four speakers,
even when they talk over each other.
A SpeakerTimeline collects its results
and attributes each timed word to a speaker,
so you can print a transcript by speaker turn.
Like image support in AnyLanguageModel,
this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today. The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default.
You can also choose v2.1 ,
which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data
and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too. How well does it work? We measured the package with its hear command-line tool
on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1.
Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes: Transcriber test-clean test-other Parakeet v3, file 1.55% 2.78% Parakeet v3, live 4.73% 4.29% Parakeet Ultra, file 1.66% 2.55% Parakeet Ultra, live 2.65% 3.28% Parakeet Unified, file 1.43% 2.19% Parakeet Unified, live 1.45% 2.42% Apple's transcriber, file 2.12% 3.97% Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio
in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file,
or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live,
with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model.
Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory.
Meetings are hard for everyone:
on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other,
every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

title: Prime Intellect Releases Prime Mega MoE: Trainable Fused MoE Kernel, 3.11x Faster Forward Pass
abstract: Prime Intellect has released Prime Mega MoE , a training extension of DeepSeek’s fused Mega MoE kernel. DeepSeek’s kernel only ran the forward pass. Prime Intellect added a fast, overlapping backward pass. That makes the fused kernel usable for training, not just inference. In its prime-rl trainer, full training steps on Qwen3 MoE models run up to 34% faster. Against TorchTitan, the gain reaches 55%. For teams training mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, that is a direct cut in GPU hours. Prime Mega MoE is a fused, overlapping MoE kernel for training from Prime Intellect. It builds on the Mega MoE kernel in DeepSeek’s open-source DeepGEMM library. In an MoE model, each token goes to a small subset of experts. Those experts sit on different GPUs. So every layer sends tokens out, runs expert math, and sends results back. This happens in the forward pass and again in the backward pass. In a standard setup, these are separate operations. The GPU sorts tokens and waits on the transport layer. Then it computes, hands results back, and waits again. Those waits are idle GPU time. DeepSeek’s Mega MoE , added to DeepGEMM in April 2026, replaces that chain with one kernel call. It fuses expert-parallel dispatch, the 2 expert linear layers, SwiGLU, and combine. While one token group is in transit, the kernel computes on a group that already arrived. It also skips intermediate tensors by using GPU-only scratch buffers. But it only shipped a forward implementation. Prime Intellect wrote the missing backward kernel, also overlapping. Supported types are BF16, MXFP8 (Blackwell only) and blockwise FP8 (Hopper only). The prime-rl config also exposes an fp8_bwd mode: BF16 forward, FP8 backward. All numbers below are self-reported by Prime Intellect. Training steps use 8×H200 nodes, FP8, 16,384-token sequences and full activation checkpointing. Each result is the mean of steps 6 to 20. Full training step, seconds (lower is better): Against TorchTitan, throughput rose from 5,337 to 7,886 tokens/s/GPU on the 30B model. On the 235B model, it rose from 1,094 to 1,697. The prime-rl baseline uses torch all-to-all plus DeepGEMM FP8 experts. Single MoE layer, milliseconds (1 node, 8×H200, EP=8, 128 experts, top-8, random routing): The pattern is clear. Forward gains are large, and backward gains are smaller. The headline “up to 3.11x” refers to the forward pass only. TorchTitan’s 41% gain comes from a different setup (B200, 671B model, BF16 baseline). It is not directly comparable. Prime Mega MoE is a dispatch backend in prime-rl. Set type = "mega_moe" under [trainer.model.moe.dispatch] . Choose precision from bf16 , mxfp8 , fp8 or fp8_bwd . The training kernels ship in a prebuilt DeepGEMM wheel from prime-kernels . The stock DeepGEMM build lacks them. Check out the Prime Mega MoE blog post , the announcement on X , and the prime-rl repo . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. title: Infini-AI-Lab Releases Hermit, an Open-Source Harness Adapter Framework for AI Agents
abstract: Infini-AI-Lab has released Hermit , an open-source harness adapter framework for AI agents. Hermit is a framework from Infini-AI-Lab that trains an external ‘harness adapter’ while the agent’s model and harness stay frozen. The first release, v0.1.0 , shipped on October 25, 2026. CMU postdoc Haizhong Zheng announced it on X on October 27. For developers, the pitch is simple: adapt Codex or Claude Code agents to new tasks without fine-tuning or forking the harness. A harness adapter is a trainable external harness. It works like a plugin with training support built in. A model adapter, such as LoRA, adapts a model. A harness adapter adapts an existing agent instead. The adapter can hold instructions, skills, memory, tools, executable code and agent coordination logic. It can even be a whole repository. Its specification says which parts are learnable and how updates get checked. The base model and harness never change. The team gives 3 reasons for this design. Many harnesses are closed-source. Editing open ones can break carefully tuned component interactions. And a learned adapter can move between compatible models and harnesses. Hermit uses an RL-style training loop . A Trainer runs a batch of tasks through the acting agent with the current adapter. A judge scores the outputs. An Evolver reads the trajectories and feedback, then proposes a new adapter. The Trainer checks it against the template and commits it as the next version. Every adapter version lives in a git tree. You can inspect, roll back or ship any version. Learner programs can run sandboxed, which requires Linux with bubblewrap. Five evolution methods ship today: GEPA , SkillOpt , MetaWorld Model (MWM), Harness² and Continual Harness . ACE and ReHarness are listed as coming soon. You can also write your own Evolver. All runs below use GLM 5.3 Flash as the acting model. The numbers come from the repo’s example READMEs and are self-reported. OfficeQA ( recipe ) asks 172 test questions about U.S. Treasury Bulletins, scored by exact match: GEPA and SkillOpt train on 50 questions and are tested frozen. Continual Harness and Harness² instead learn while streaming the test set once. The team reports a +7.6 point gain for Harness² over its reference run, with a 95% interval of +1.7 to +13.4. CL-Bench ( database , poker ) tests stateful environments from the Continual Learning Bench paper . On database exploration, MWM reaches 0.795 accuracy. The benchmark’s in-context baseline scores 0.580. On exploitable poker, MWM wins 3.08 big blinds per hand, vs 2.51 for in-context learning. ServeLearnBench ( recipe ) streams 624 retail support requests under a hidden, shifting policy. MWM scores 45.3 on hidden-policy tests. The best learning method on the leaderboard, CH, scores 28.7. An oracle given the policy scores 89.2. Install from PyPI with pip install hermit-harness , or clone the repo for examples. The CLI covers check , train , eval , deploy and convert . Models are referenced as <backend>/<model id> . Supported backends include Fireworks, OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, vLLM, SGLang and Ollama. hermit deploy writes a workspace for Codex, Claude Code or Pi. hermit convert exports a trained adapter as a native plugin for Codex, Claude Code, Pi or Hermes. A finished Lean collaboration adapter coordinates 5 Codex agents proving one theorem together. Check out the GitHub repo , project page and docs . title: Block Unveils Dessa, a Full-Duplex Speech Model Trained Only on Speech
abstract: Block’s AI research lab has released Dessa , a full-duplex speech model trained only on human conversation. Block announced it on October 23, 2026 as a research preview. Dessa is a speech-to-speech model from Block that listens and talks at the same time. Block says it used no text and no pretrained models. That is a different design from the text-first stacks behind most voice agents today. Dessa is a true speech-to-speech model: audio in, audio out. According to Block’s project page , everything it knows came from human speech. It is full-duplex, so it listens while it talks. Block says it learned from real conversation when to cut in. It also learned when to backchannel with short cues like “yeah” or “got it”. Block’s demo clips show Dessa laughing mid-sentence and getting louder when asked to speak up. One clip shows it talking with OpenAI’s GPT-Live-1. Block says nobody steered any clip. Most voice systems chain 3 parts: speech recognition, a text model, then speech synthesis. Block team argues that chain throws away emotion, sarcasm, laughter and sighs. Dessa hears and produces those signals directly. Block has not published the architecture. Here is what it has disclosed: The lab also explains why this is hard. Speech never repeats exactly. A spoken word takes thousands of times more bytes than the same word in text. Kyutai’s Moshi, the best-known open full-duplex model, takes another route. Moshi starts from a text language model backbone and predicts time-aligned text tokens before audio tokens. Its model card lists 7 million hours of pretraining audio and 1,016 H100 GPUs. Check out the Dessa project page . Compare it with the Moshi paper , the PersonaPlex model card and the GPT-Live-1 docs . title: AssemblyAI Ships AssemblyAI-TTS-1: A $15 per 1M Character Text-to-Speech API for Voice Agents
abstract: AssemblyAI has released AssemblyAI-TTS-1 , its first text-to-speech model, now generally available. The AssemblyAI-TTS-1 text-to-speech API targets voice agents running on live phone calls. In that setting, latency and pronunciation decide whether a caller stays on the line. Pricing is $15 per 1M characters , with no annual contract and no concurrency tier to buy. For developers already using AssemblyAI speech-to-text, it closes the voice loop with one vendor. AssemblyAI-TTS-1 is a streaming text-to-speech model from AssemblyAI that turns agent replies into speech for live calls. It was trained on millions of hours of audio , including real conversational data. Most TTS models represent audio as discrete tokens. AssemblyAI says TTS-1 operates on continuous audio representations instead. The AssemblyAI claims this improves realism and cuts time to first spoken audio. The launch includes a library of 4,000+ voices and instant voice cloning. A clone needs a short recording and a confirmation of the speaker’s permission. The clone in the launch post used 24 seconds of audio. Six languages are supported at launch: English, Spanish, French, German, Italian and Portuguese. There are 3 interfaces: an HTTP API, a WebSocket API and an OpenAI-compatible route . The WebSocket session keeps one connection per conversation and accepts a cancel message for barge-in. Output is mono PCM, mu-law or A-law, at 8 kHz to 48 kHz. 24 kHz PCM is the native format; telephony stacks can request 8 kHz mu-law directly. Word timestamps are included. AssemblyAI also published LiveKit and Pipecat reference agents. AssemblyAI tested TTS-1 against 5 models on 4 English sets, using 50 matched cloned voices. All figures below are self-reported , from an eval dated October 28, 2026. Independent results are more mixed. On Cekura’s benchmark of 27 models, TTS-1 scored 81.5% reading accuracy and 4.50 naturalness. Its median streaming latency, timed from the last word sent, was 159 ms. Inworld TTS-2 Flash posted 45 ms and 93.2% accuracy there, at the same $15 price. AssemblyAI also cites a 1.7% word error rate on Coval’s leaderboard . It reports a top-10 debut in Artificial Analysis’ controlled-voice arena. Cartesia’s range divides each plan price by its credits, at 1 credit per character. Pricing is per input character, including spaces and punctuation, at $15 per 1M . Every voice, cloning, word timestamps and EU processing come at that same rate. There are no per-voice fees, concurrency fees or minimums. AssemblyAI calls it the lowest-priced frontier TTS model for voice agents. However, Inworld TTS-2 Flash also lists $15 per 1M on demand, falling to $7 on paid plans. The sharper difference is concurrency: Inworld’s on-demand tier allows 5 concurrent requests. Check out the launch post , docs , pricing , and the LiveKit and Pipecat reference agents. title: NVIDIA Releases Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe: An Open 30B MoE Model for 40-Language Transcription with ~4B Active Parameters
abstract: NVIDIA has released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe , an open-weights speech LLM built for transcription. One model handles 40 languages and recordings up to 1 hour . A text instruction picks the output style for each request. Options include verbatim, written form, speaker-attributed, contextual and translated output. For developers, it can replace separate ASR, diarization and alignment tools. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is a speech-augmented language model (SALM) from NVIDIA that turns audio and instructions into text. An audio encoder feeds embeddings into an LLM decoder, which makes transcription promptable. NVIDIA’s technical research report argues there is no single correct transcript. Numbers, fillers and domain terms depend on who reads the output. NVIDIA positions the model as a transcription specialist, not a general-purpose assistant. The model name says 30B-A4B, but the checkpoint holds about 34B parameters. The extra weight comes from the 1.3B MTP module and the audio components. Training used 1 supervised fine-tuning stage on 256 H100 GPUs for 28,500 steps. A short RL stage followed: 400 GSPO updates with a reward of 1 minus WER. The model saw about 1.72M unique hours of audio, or 6.5M hours with repeats. All numbers below are self-reported by NVIDIA in the technical report . Weights ship in BF16 , FP8 , NVFP4 and GGUF . A DFlash2 draft model is optional. The OpenMDW-1.1 license allows commercial use. Runtimes include vLLM 0.32.0 with the NeMo Speech plugin, Transformers and SGLang-Omni 0.2.0. vLLM exposes an OpenAI-compatible API. NVIDIA model’s main speed comes from its Nemotron Transcribe NIM. With NVFP4 and DFlash2, 1 RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition transcribes 2,238 seconds of audio per second. It returns a 30-second clip in 0.13 seconds. There is a catch: those serving optimizations are not open source yet. NVIDIA expects the release-day vLLM path to be roughly 2x slower. On 1 H100 in BF16 with MTP2, NVIDIA estimates about 410 RTFx. For fine-tuning, NVIDIA tested 17 tasks. Each took about 0.5 to 2.3 GPU-hours on a single GB300. *Competitor scores on the current 9-set leaderboard come from NVIDIA’s report, citing Hugging Face leaderboard results from October 2026. The leaderboard set changed since the competitors published their own cards, so the 2 WER rows are not interchangeable. Check out the technical report , model weights , project page and live demo .
