title: Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale
abstract: Every code change improves our platform, but it also introduces new complexity. With hundreds of millions of lines of code constantly evolving at Meta, traditional testing can’t keep pace. Catching risks proactively, before code lands, enables us to identify risks earlier, respond more effectively, and deliver reliable experiences at scale. Over the last year, we’ve shared our research into applying large language models (LLMs) to generate software tests . More specifically, we’ve shared our work with Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests) , a novel testing approach where we leverage LLMs to catch bugs on the fly, even ones that traditional testing might not catch. In the five months since we first unveiled this work, we’ve deployed our Catching JiTTests approach to determine its scalability and applicability to the wider industry. Today, Catching JiTTests are no longer a research prototype; they’re part of Meta’s infrastructure, and they’re helping our engineers catch more bugs with less load and a smaller chance of false positives. Most AI-based approaches to preventing bugs in code use LLMs and/or agentic AI to review code and detect faults based on prior experience. They work through the same review process that a human reviewer would, only faster. Catching JiTTests is a fundamentally different approach (Table 1): It generates executable tests that demonstrate a concrete behavioral difference introduced by the change. While it requires more computational steps, it catches classes of bugs that LLM- or agent-based code reviews might not. JiTTests are automatically generated and designed to fail, surfacing bugs in code changes (diffs) before they land in production. When they’re applied to a codebase as large as Meta’s, one challenge is distinguishing strong catches (i.e., true-positive failures that reveal real bugs) from weak catches (i.e., tests that may be false positives). It boils down to a specific question: For every proposed diff, how can we automatically generate tests that find the most severe bugs before they cause severe issues, and do so with a high true-positive rate and without impeding the velocity of our engineers? To address this, we developed two tandem workflows: To filter false positives, we employed a traditional rule-based approach combined with an ensemble approach we call “LLM-as-Judge,” which aggregates judgements from several state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs, all tasked with classifying weak catches as likely true or false positives. We also maintained human review, with an eye toward reducing review load. Our goal is to maintain the consistency of human labeling but reduce the likelihood of an engineer being brought in to review a weak catch. The entire system workflow happens in five stages: The system runs overnight on spare capacity and targets diffs submitted the previous day that are deemed “risky” using a mechanism similar to Diff Risk Score (DRS) and trained on previous code changes. This helps ensure test generation is focused on diffs that are most likely to contain severe regressions. The dodgy diff workflow treats each diff as if it were a mutant and uses mutation-guided LLM-based test generation to produce tests that distinguish the diff’s behavior from its parent. The goal here is to maximize the pool of weak catches and with it the chances of finding a strong catch among them. At the same time, the intent-aware workflow uses an LLM to infer the diff’s intention using the code changes, diff title, and summary. The LLM then describes the “risks” — the ways an attempt to implement the intent could produce errors. It then uses those risk descriptions to construct mutants — each representing a bug that could be introduced while implementing the inferred intent. Tests are generated to kill each mutant (i.e., distinguish mutant behavior from parent). Those tests are then run on the actual diff. Any that fail are harvested as weak catches. Once weak catches are generated, the system must determine whether each is a false positive or actually a strong catch (true positive). The LLM-as-Judge ensemble consists of a collection of LLMs that review: We complement LLM-as-Judge with a more traditional, rule-based approach called Rule-Based False-Positive Killing Environment (RubFake). LLM-as-Judge has rich semantics, but its judgements are non-deterministic and challenging to verify. By contrast, RubFake provides verified, deterministic judgments. Working together, RubFake and LLM-as-Judge produce an overall ranking of weak-catch candidates, with those ranked sufficiently highly being worthy of further consideration. Based on the ranking from LLM-as-Judge and RubFake, the system then decides whether to reach out to human engineers. Rather than a human-in-the-loop approach, where a human engineer reviews every output, we’ve reduced friction through a human- on -the-loop approach, where human engineers set criteria and review outcomes at an aggregate level rather than supervising every output. With the testing system in place, our goal is to get engineers to engage with its results. As of this writing, 589 engineers at Meta (64% of our outreach) have engaged with Catching JiTTests. These engineers have reported that Catching JiTTests surfaces genuinely actionable findings, with a 60% rate of true positives. In the first half of 2026, Catching JiTTests played a key role in catching 74 serious (SEV) privacy bugs at the diff stage, before they landed in production and lowering the overall occurrence of privacy SEVs by 20% during that timeframe. Agentic software development is helping engineers and developers across the industry write, review, and ship code faster than ever before. But faster deployment means there’s also a need for faster testing. Every bug caught before it reaches production is one that end users never need to deal with. We’ve shown that LLMs can provide an additional safety layer capable of catching what traditional tests may miss, demonstrating that AI-generated testing can scale enough to reduce organizational risk. Catching JiTTests is a solution that is scalable, both technologically and socially. Combining these tests with a human-on-the-loop approach helps ensure that engineers rarely need to read test code and only need to confirm whether an observed behavioral change was intended. The approach is generalizable: Engineers define success criteria early, let AI execute the testing, monitor the outcomes at an aggregate level, and intervene at the policy level rather than per item. Our paper, “ Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta ,” which was presented at FSE 2026 and featured at Product@Scale , details our initial deployment and testing with Catching JiTTests in Meta’s infrastructure. The post Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale appeared first on Engineering at Meta .

title: Unlocking Tensor Core Performance for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
abstract: Atomistic simulations help researchers understand how molecules and materials behave, from chemical reactions and phase transitions to mechanical failure. These simulations come with a cost-accuracy trade-off. Quantum-mechanical methods such as density functional theory (DFT) can provide accurate energies and forces, but their computational cost often limits their use for large systems or long simulations. Classical interatomic potentials are much faster, but their fixed functional forms limit accuracy and generalizability across different atomic environments. Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) help bridge this gap. They use neural networks to predict potential energies and interatomic forces at a fraction of the cost, enabling researchers to study larger systems and longer timescales while retaining much of the required accuracy. Running an MLIP efficiently, however, presents its own challenge. Atomistic simulations are sensitive to small errors that can accumulate over time and are most visible when computing forces, which are obtained by differentiating the predicted energy. During molecular dynamics simulations, these forces guide updates to atomic velocities and positions over many timesteps, making numerical precision important not only for physical accuracy but also for the stability of the resulting trajectory. For this reason, many MLIPs continue to run inference in FP32, even though modern NVIDIA GPUs offer substantially higher matrix-multiplication throughput through low-precision Tensor Core operations. Tensor Core methods for FP32 matrix multiplication offer a way to narrow that gap. They decompose each FP32 operand into lower-precision components, evaluate their cross-products on Tensor Cores, and recombine the results in FP32. This approach can increase matrix-multiplication throughput while retaining accuracy close to native FP32, without retraining or changing the model’s weights or architecture. In this post, we evaluate how Tensor Core FP32 methods perform in practice on the Point Edge Transformer (PET), a transformer-based MLIP developed by Lab COSMO at EPFL. PET spends much of its runtime in highly optimized general matrix multiplications (GEMMs), leaving limited headroom for further optimization and making it a demanding test case of whether these methods can deliver additional performance gains. We evaluate BF16x9 on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs and TF32x3 on NVIDIA Ampere GPUs, comparing kernel and end-to-end molecular dynamics performance and trajectory-level behavior. We further test the TF32x3 method for potential-energy smoothness, energy conservation, and structural relaxation. We show how these methods can accelerate MLIP inference while retaining behavior close to the FP32 baseline and outline how to evaluate them on other precision-sensitive scientific machine learning workloads. How Tensor Core FP32 closes the hardware gap Modern NVIDIA GPUs deliver substantially higher Tensor Core throughput for BF16 and TF32 than for FP32 matrix multiplication, creating a gap between the available throughput at lower precision and the precision requirements of many scientific workloads. Tensor Core FP32 methods help narrow this gap by decomposing FP32 operands into lower-precision components, evaluating selected products on Tensor Cores, and recombining them with FP32 accumulation. Depending on the method and workload, this can deliver accuracy at or near native FP32 while taking advantage of higher Tensor Core throughput. Figure 1. The BF16x9 algorithm on Blackwell GPUs. Each FP32 operand is split into three scaled BF16 components, producing nine pairwise products that are accumulated in FP32 along five anti-diagonal bands On Blackwell GPUs, NVIDIA cuBLAS provides a BF16x9 Tensor Core path (Figure 1). Each FP32 operand is decomposed into three BF16 components, and nine pairwise products are recombined with the required scaling. cuBLAS can enable this path through the CUBLAS_EMULATE_SINGLE_PRECISION=1 environment variable, so compatible PyTorch GEMMs can use it without changing the model architecture or implementing a custom GEMM. Because this approach changes how GEMMs are evaluated, it may provide additional gains when combined with optimized graph construction, fused operations, custom kernels, and NVIDIA CUDA graphs. We did not measure the combined gain in this evaluation; it should be established end to end for each workload. Figure 2. The TF32x3 algorithm on Ampere GPUs. Each FP32 operand is split into a leading TF32 component and a smaller residual component. The leading-by-leading and two leading-by-residual products are accumulated in FP32; the residual-by-residual product is omitted The TF32x3 method applies the same principle on Ampere GPUs (Figure 2). TF32x3 represents each FP32 operand using a leading TF32 component and a residual TF32 component. Unlike BF16x9, our TF32x3 implementation does not use scaling factors. It evaluates three cross-products and omits the residual-by-residual term, as shown in the following equation a ⋅ b ≈ a hi b hi + a hi b lo + a lo b hi a \cdot b \approx a_{\mathrm{hi}}b_{\mathrm{hi}} + a_{\mathrm{hi}}b_{\mathrm{lo}} + a_{\mathrm{lo}}b_{\mathrm{hi}} NVIDIA CUTLASS provides this approach through the OpMultiplyAddFastF32 operator. Inputs and outputs remain in FP32. Tensor Cores execute the three TF32 products with accumulation in FP32. Benchmarking Tensor Core FP32 matrix math on PET We evaluated the 26M-parameter PET-MAD small checkpoint ( pet-mad-s-v1.6.0-nn-32 ) on a 192-atom water box and a 17,280-atom supercell. We also evaluated the 255M-parameter large checkpoint ( pet-mad-m-v1.6.0 ) on the 192-atom system. We compared predicted energies, forces, and stresses with those from the native FP32 path. BF16x9 method on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs On NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with compute capability 10.0 or 10.3, cuBLAS supports enabling BF16x9 through an environment variable, math mode, or compute type (requested with CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F_EMULATED_16BFX9 , CUBLAS_FP32_EMULATED_BF16X9_MATH , or CUBLAS_EMULATE_SINGLE_PRECISION=1 ). No model-code changes are required to use this path for single-precision general matrix multiplication (SGEMM). Figure 3. With BF16x9 Tensor Core math for SGEMMs, large GEMMs in the PET model were accelerated by 2.2–2.5x for the 17,280-atom workload and 1.2–1.4x for the 192-atom workload Figure 4. MD-step speedup and single-point energy and force accuracy for cuBLAS’s performant and eager BF16x9 modes, relative to compiled FP32, on a 192-atom water box and its 17,280-atom supercell With BF16x9 on Blackwell, large GEMMs in PET were accelerated by 2.2–2.5x for the 17,280-atom workload (Figure 3). Figure 4 compares MD-step speedup and single-point energy and force accuracy for cuBLAS’s performant and eager strategies against compiled FP32. 192-atom system: The performant strategy sped up the MD step by 1.2x, while the eager strategy achieved 1.1x. 17,280-atom system: The performant strategy achieved a 1.7x speedup, while the eager strategy achieved 1.4x. The performant strategy uses BF16x9 when cuBLAS expects it to be faster; the eager strategy uses it whenever the operation supports it. Importantly, the error due to the BF16x9 Tensor Core method is below the model’s own level of non-determinism. This result is significant because PET already expresses much of its runtime as optimized GEMM work, and yet the BF16x9 path exposed performance headroom without retraining the model, changing its transformer architecture, or writing custom kernels. TF32x3 method on Ampere GPUs On Ampere GPUs, we implemented TF32x3 by replacing PET’s standard nn.Linear layers with a custom TF32Linear layer that calls a CUTLASS C++ TF32x3 kernel. CUTLASS C++ provides a reference implementation of this approach in Example 27 . The key setting in the PET implementation is: C++ cutlass::arch::OpMultiplyAddFastF32 This selects CUTLASS’s fast, accurate FP32 multiplication mode.

title: How the UK Amazon Quick User Group grew in 2026
abstract: The Amazon Quick User Group – United Kingdom is a community of Amazon Quick users in the United Kingdom who meet quarterly to exchange knowledge, share best practices, learn through hands-on sessions, and discuss their experiences using the service. These user groups function as collaborative forums where members learn, connect, and innovate together. Whether you’re already using Amazon Quick or just getting started, we’d love for you to join the UK Amazon Quick User Group and become part of a growing community that’s redefining how organizations make decisions with data. In this post, we’re thrilled to share our 2026 yearly roundup, highlighting all three quarterly meetups that have taken place since the group’s launch and the momentum that has followed. The events drew more than 150 attendees, and the energy in the room, fueled by agentic AI and the potential of Amazon Quick, was clear. Across industries, customers are using Amazon Quick to turn data chaos into faster decisions, higher satisfaction, and scalable growth. Their work spans real-time incident management, eliminating dashboard sprawl with governed data layers, and automating most support workflows with AI. The UK Amazon Quick User Group is a local community of Amazon Quick users who come together quarterly to share knowledge, best practices, and experiences with the service. Amazon Quick user groups serve as collaborative forums where members can: Over three quarterly meetups this year, the UK community spent real time with Amazon Quick. Not slide decks about it, actual time building with it. People created Amazon Quick custom chat agents for their teams without writing code. They tried Amazon Quick Desktop running on their own laptops, connected to local files and using a connector to access Outlook. They also used Amazon Quick Apps to turn a plain-language description into a working web application. The workshops had attendees automating processes with Amazon Quick Flows and Amazon Quick Automate , while Amazon Quick Research showed how it significantly cuts down the time spent on research. The Amazon Quick chat agent tied it together, an assistant that connects to tools, data and takes actions on your behalf. Every quarter, the sessions got more practical and the questions from the room got sharper. All three events were held at the Amazon UK Corporate Office in Shoreditch, London. By 9:45 AM, the room is already buzzing. People reconnect over coffee, swap updates from the last quarter, and newcomers get pulled into conversations before the day even officially begins. From there, the energy carries through the full agenda: customers share real stories about what they’ve built with Amazon Quick, product leads walk through the latest updates, and panels spark the kind of back-and-forth you don’t get from a webinar. The 75-minute hands-on workshop is where it really comes alive, with attendees rolling up their sleeves in provisioned sandbox accounts and experimenting together. By the time we close with a feedback session, the room feels more like a working group than an audience. The format has shifted each quarter. Q1 leaned more on introductions and demos because the group was meeting for the first time. By Q2, we added an icebreaker quiz, and ran a focused workshop on Quick Flows and automation. For Q3 we brought in a specialist panel, a group quiz, and a networking slot at the end. That last one came about because people were already staying behind to talk after the close, so we stopped packing up around them and put it in the schedule. Figure 1: Attendees at a UK Amazon Quick User Group meetup Customer stories have been part of the community from the start. Each speaker brought a different problem into the room, showing how teams are applying Quick in very different environments. At the first event, the conversation centered on getting insight into the hands of the people who need it. At Arriva UK Trains, critical data wasn’t reaching the people who needed it most. Train and station managers were constantly on the move, relying solely on their work mobiles. Sofia Bourika’s team built dynamic, role-based dashboards with mobile-friendly views and introduced pixel perfect reports automatically delivered through scheduled email, giving managers immediate visibility of incidents and performance. The result: faster decisions, better incident management, and a stronger data-driven culture across the organization. By Q2, the discussion had moved toward a different challenge: getting the foundations right before introducing more AI and automation. At Carsa , a used-car retailer, analytics functioned like a service desk. Question in, dashboard out. The same question gave different answers. It wasn’t a data problem. It was a definitions problem. Tobi Daramola’s team at Carsa fixed this by building a single governed data layer, with metrics defined once and consumed by Amazon Quick and AI assistants alike. As a result, they removed 50 percent of dashboards while surfacing more data. Customer satisfaction (CSAT) scores moved 10 percent in 30 days, complaints same-day close rate jumped 20 percent, and AI on the layer cut recurring tasks from 45 minutes to 5. Q3 brought the conversation further into automation and agentic workflows. Propulse Lab , a Swiss operating system for B2C subscription businesses, was handling 1 million support tickets a year. Their teams were stuck firefighting instead of driving growth. After deploying a multi-agent AI pipeline in Amazon Quick Automate, built from their best past customer service interactions, they cut request handling from 7 minutes to 70 seconds. The pipeline also automated 80 percent of routine workflows. “What was once a cost centre became a growth engine – their product managers now own the entire system without writing a single line of code, and their support teams focus on proactive, revenue-driving conversations instead.” — Guirec Lecointre, Growth Operations Specialist, Propulse Lab The use cases vary widely, and that’s exactly the point. Rather than presenting a single vision for Amazon Quick, practitioners show what they’ve tried against real business problems, from governed analytics and frontline reporting to automation and AI. That shifts the conversation in the room. Attendees ask direct questions about implementation, adoption, and what didn’t work. Speakers share the practical lessons behind the finished solution. People leave with ideas they can apply to their own organizations, not just another customer story. Attendees changed across the three events. A listen-and-learn turned into building meaningful relationships by Q3. People were new to the group and new to each other. By Q2, the icebreaker quiz loosened things up early. The feedback sessions got more specific too: instead of “this was great,” people were requesting topics and offering to contribute. Q3 pushes this further. Sofia Bourika, who joined the leadership team early on and presented the Arriva customer story at the first event, came up with an icebreaker called “What Are You Proud Of?”, attendees share something they’ve built with Amazon Quick. We’ve already got someone who was previously sitting in the audience volunteering to present their work. That kind of shift, from attending to contributing, took three events to happen, but it happened. Q3 also introduced a new segment, the Amazon Quick specialist panel. Questions were pre-collected from the audience and posed to an invited specialist, who brought real depth to the answers and shared first-hand experience of working with attendees’ customers. It sparked a different kind of thinking in the room, with the audience connecting the dots between the specialist’s insights and their own day-to-day challenges. Our community stayed connected all year. Our LinkedIn group had weekly contributions and our email lists encouraged involvement.

title: Building intent-driven UI testing with Amazon Nova Act
abstract: To scale intent-driven UI testing across its product teams, Epsilon , a data, technology, and marketing-services company and part of Publicis Groupe , turned to Amazon Nova Act . With hundreds of millions of consumer profiles and thousands of brand relationships, Epsilon needed UI testing that could keep pace with rapid application changes. The solution could not create maintenance overhead for every product team. Within Epsilon, the Agentic Platform team (50 engineers) builds shared infrastructure so other product teams can build, deploy, govern, and run AI agents safely. With this shared platform, teams get a skills-based agent builder. They also get federated identity and pre-flight authorization, Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration, and cross-account provisioning. When a product team wants to adopt AI tooling, they get capabilities without additional configuration and without re-solving identity, security, browser infrastructure, or model integration on their own. One of those managed capabilities is UI testing . With Amazon Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), Epsilon’s platform team could deliver resilient, intent-driven testing as a service to teams on the platform. In this post, we walk through Epsilon’s architecture for delivering UI testing as a managed platform service, show the core Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool integration code, highlight a concrete 18-step test workflow, and share best practices and measured results. Epsilon’s existing UI testing practice was not broken. The team maintained a Playwright-based regression suite that validated functionality across their web applications, and it worked well. Playwright remains their regression backbone today. The opportunity Epsilon identified was additive, not corrective: The goal: layer intent-based testing on top of the existing Playwright regression suite. Deliver it as a multi-tenant platform service so that each Epsilon product team could consume through the same API surface they used for every other agent capability. Epsilon evaluated options against two requirements: natural-language test authoring (to complement selector-based Playwright tests) and managed browser infrastructure (to fit their multi-tenant platform model). With Amazon Nova Act combined with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, Epsilon could address both. Epsilon chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool specifically because it eliminates the operational burden of managing browser binaries, display servers, and session lifecycle. The Agentic Platform team had no interest in owning that infrastructure. Epsilon’s solution has three main components: a platform API for creating workflows, a background task runner for executing them, and the Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool integration that drives the browser. Epsilon’s UI testing capability follows a clear pipeline: Figure 1: Epsilon’s UI Testing Service architecture Figure 1 shows the layered architecture of Epsilon’s UI Testing Service. User requests flow from the Agent Cloud Frontend through an API Gateway with authentication and permission checks. The API layer (Django REST) exposes endpoints for workflows, executions, automation suites, and stats. The business logic layer includes a Workflow Manager, Execution Orchestrator, and Suite Coordinator. Test jobs are queued in Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) and picked up by the Runner Service running on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), which contains the Nova Act engine and a headless Chromium browser. Results, screenshots, trajectories, and HTML reports are stored in Amazon S3. The capability is exposed as a standard agent ( ui-test-agent ) with two skills: Onboarded teams consume UI testing the same way they consume any other platform agent. No additional infrastructure to manage. The onboarding process is straightforward. The platform team provisions a cross-account IAM role for the new team, registers their target application URLs, and grants access to the ui-test-agent through the existing platform API. From that point, teams create workflows, trigger executions, and retrieve results through the same interface they already use for other platform capabilities. The Nova Act + Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool integration is concise: This pattern (open a managed browser session, connect through the CDP WebSocket, and drive actions with natural language) is the foundation. Epsilon wraps it with their platform’s multi-tenant orchestration, result capture, and observability layers. To illustrate intent-based testing, here is a representative workflow from Epsilon’s platform. It exercises login, form entry, conditional handling, scrolling, and verification. The following steps highlight the differentiating patterns of Nova Act: Steps 4 and 7 demonstrate conditional logic : “if an element appears, handle it” and “if a target isn’t visible, scroll until it is.” These patterns would require explicit branching in a traditional framework. Nova Act handles them naturally through language understanding. Epsilon runs UI tests in a dedicated runner service (a FastAPI sidecar) that pins nova-act 3.x with Workflow and IAM authentication support, plus the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool client. This keeps dependencies separate from the main backend so they don’t collide with the Strands agent stack. The worker falls back to in-process execution if the runner is disabled, providing resilience during deployments. Based on their experience building UI testing as a platform capability, the Epsilon team recommends: Intent-based steps survive UI redesigns. Product managers and quality assurance (QA) leads who might not write code can review them directly. Pin Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool dependencies in a dedicated service or container. Epsilon learned that the signing endpoint for Nova Act targets us-east-1 regardless of the browser session’s region. Running it in a separate service with its own dependency lockfile prevents hard-to-debug conflicts. Epsilon uses trajectory retries in draft state , saves the successful trajectory, and replays it in active state . Repeat runs skip redundant large language model (LLM) “thinking,” reducing both latency and cost for regression-style repeated executions. Use cross-account AssumeRole with scoped IAM policies. Each tenant’s tests run under their own role in their own account. This provides isolation, auditability, and failure scope containment without custom infrastructure per team. With Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, teams get live view, session recording, and AWS CloudTrail integration. Epsilon uses these built-in capabilities instead of building custom observability, reducing maintenance and giving compliance teams familiar audit surfaces. When prompting Nova Act steps, account for the browser viewport defaults of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool. Steps that reference scrolling (for example, “scroll down until the Goal Statement textbox is visible”) verify that Nova Act handles content in the lower portion of the page correctly. Epsilon’s UI testing capability is operational across multiple teams, with the multi-tenant architecture proven in production. Here are the measured outcomes: “Nova Act let us turn UI testing from a brittle, selector-chasing chore into a managed platform capability. Our tests now describe intent in plain English, run on AWS managed browsers, and every product team we onboard gets reliable testing without additional configuration.” — Epsilon Agentic Platform Team Epsilon’s Agentic Platform team demonstrated how to deliver resilient, intent-driven UI testing as a managed service using Amazon Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool. You can apply the same pattern to your own multi-tenant platform to eliminate browser infrastructure overhead and make test authoring accessible to non-engineers.

title: Build a repeatable PHP-to-Java migration engine with Kiro
abstract: When your team moves a mature PHP application to Java, you gain stronger type safety, broader library support, and more predictable scaling. A PHP codebase built over the years with Laravel, Symfony, or Doctrine carries business rules in places that are not obvious, from Eloquent traits to XML mapping files, so a structurally similar Java port can compile cleanly and still behave differently. This post shows how to turn PHP-to-Java migration from a one-time leap of faith into a measurable, repeatable process using Kiro . Kiro is an AI integrated development environment (IDE) that pairs an AI agent with your codebase to run multi-step engineering tasks with you in the loop. The approach centers on a reusable engine: a shared methodology, a mechanical discovery scanner, and an eight-phase workflow. This engine treats the original PHP application as the specification and refuses to declare the Java port correct until a parity harness verifies it. Before getting started, you need: You start with an open repository, so you can run the engine yourself rather than read about it. Everything the engine knows lives in a small set of skill files, and with those files, you can run the same methodology in more than one way. Everything here is packaged as skill files: versioned Markdown capability packages that encode the migration methodology (php-to-java-migration) and the discovery scanner workflow (php-model-discovery). Because that knowledge lives in files rather than any one tool, you can run the same methodology in two ways. Kiro brings an AI agent into your editor to drive a migration step by step. Open the repository root as a Kiro workspace and the skills activate automatically when you ask Kiro to migrate a PHP application. Kiro then walks the eight-phase workflow with explicit approval gates, so you review the discovery manifest, approve the rulebook, and sign off on each phase before the next begins. It’s the mode used for every example in this post. AWS Transform is the AWS agentic AI service for large-scale migration and modernization, and it now integrates natively with Kiro. Through that integration, you can hand AWS Transform the same skill files that govern an interactive Kiro session, so discovery before translation, the parity harness as referee, and ‘ fix the loop, not the code ’ apply to an autonomous run. The engine is organized around a single principle: one shared brain, many projects. To open it, clone the repository locally, then in Kiro open a folder and select the repository root (the folder containing .kiro/). Kiro loads the skills and steering automatically, with fuller steps in “Getting started.” The workspace separates a shared methodology layer from the individual projects that use it, as shown in the following diagram. At the top is a global .kiro/ layer that every project draws on. Beneath it sit the per-project folders, each with its own PHP source, Java output, and specification sub-folder. Figure 1: The workspace is split into a shared, global methodology layer and per-project code and spec folders Those same shared skill files can be run in two different ways, shown in the following diagram. The identical eight-phase, parity-first pipeline can be driven either by Kiro (interactive, one application at a time) or by AWS Transform (agentic, at portfolio scale), and both convert PHP source into parity-verified Spring Boot Java. Figure 2: The same shared skill files drive two execution paths: Kiro (interactive, one app at a time) and AWS Transform (agentic, portfolio scale). Both run the identical eight-phase parity-first pipeline, converting PHP source into parity-verified Spring Boot Java A shared, global layer under .kiro/ holds two Skills, php-model-discovery (the scanner) and php-to-java-migration (the eight-phase playbook), plus the core-workflow.md Steering file. Each per-project folder holds its own PHP source, Java output, and spec sub-folder under .kiro/specs/, so improving the methodology once lets every project inherit the gain. The single most important rule fires before anything else: Don’t read, guess at, or hand-translate a model or entity file until the scanner has run. The scanner works in a single pass with no dependencies, as shown in the following diagram. It applies three discovery strategies to the source tokens and emits one JSON manifest, with anything ambiguous routed to a review-flag queue for a human to resolve. Figure 3: The scanner runs three discovery strategies over source tokens and emits a single JSON manifest with a review-flag queue The scanner is discover-models.php, a single-file, dependency-free PHP command-line tool that doesn’t execute the target code. It only reads source text as tokens, so it runs against apps of your choice whether its dependencies are installed. It runs three strategies on every scan: Eloquent model discovery (walking the class inheritance chain to Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Model), Doctrine attribute detection (the #[ORM\Entity] attribute), and ORM XML mapping (external *.orm.xml files). The output is a single JSON manifest. A models[] array carries every field, cast, relationship, and visibility rule, and a flags[] array appears on every entry. The scanner flags ambiguity rather than guessing. For example, a $fillable list built from a runtime expression becomes a plain-English flag, and that flag list is the human review queue. Phase 0 is preparatory: it runs the scanner and assembles the inventory. The first three phases then concentrate human expertise. Phase 1 builds the parity harness before Java is written, replaying request/response pairs against both the PHP original and the Java port. The harness must pass against working PHP and fail when you break it deliberately, because a harness that misses injected breakage is not trusted. Phase 2 seeds the rulebook and gap inventory (RULEBOOK.md, GAP_INVENTORY.md), and Phase 3 stress-tests it against representative files before committing it across the application. Figure 4: Human judgment is front-loaded into a preparatory Phase 0 and Phases 1–3. Phases 4–8 are mostly self-driving loops, refereed by a parity harness The first four phases concentrate human expertise. Phase 0 runs the scanner and assembles the inventory. Phase 1 builds the parity harness before Java is written, replaying request/response pairs against both the PHP original and the Java port. The harness must pass against working PHP and fail when you break it deliberately, because a harness that misses injected breakage is not trusted. Phase 2 seeds the rulebook and gap inventory (RULEBOOK.md, GAP_INVENTORY.md), and Phase 3 stress-tests it against representative files before committing it across the application. Phases 4–8 are mostly self-driving loops: Phase 4 scaffolds the project, Phase 5 translates the data model from the manifest, Phase 6 translates the I/O layer (routes become controllers, middleware becomes filters, validation becomes annotated data transfer objects), Phase 7 converts business logic in batches, and Phase 8 proves parity against the harness and cuts over. Two principles govern the loop. First, the PHP code is the specification: the port is done when the referee agrees, or each mismatch is logged as an approved change. Second, you fix the loop, not the code, amending the rulebook and regenerating rather than hand-patching. The laravel-eloquent-sample project is a working, bounded example: a read-only slice of an open source Laravel application, with the Book, Chapter, Page, and User models migrated to Spring Boot 3.4.1 on Java 21 with Maven and an in-memory H2 database. The mapping from PHP to Spring Boot is mechanical and traceable, as shown in the following diagram. Each manifest entry on the left maps to a Java construct on the right, producing the layered runtime architecture of the generated application slice. Figure 5: Manifest-driven mappings on the left.

title: Lend and borrow resources across teams with AWS Batch’s quota management for SageMaker Training jobs
abstract: With the launch of AWS Batch support for Amazon SageMaker Training jobs, customers gained a new fully managed way to queue, schedule, and retry machine learning (ML) training workloads without building their own infrastructure. Instead, they use the queuing and scheduling features of AWS Batch. As organizations scale their artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) operations and onboard more teams, coordinating access to shared graphics processing unit (GPU) capacity can introduce additional communication, coordination, and configuration overhead for administrators. This overhead includes setting up separate queues, adjusting capacity limits, and carefully orchestrating the right workloads to get the right resources at the right time. A core value proposition of AWS Batch is helping customers increase utilization of their compute, and as training environments grow, so does the opportunity to do more with existing capacity. Working backward from customers managing multi-team training environments, we heard a consistent request: give us a way to define allocations per team or project, share idle capacity automatically, and run our highest-priority workloads first. This request led us to build quota management , a new scheduling capability for AWS Batch. Administrators can use it to divide compute capacity into quota shares, organized by team, project, or workload. Each quota share uses configurable resource-sharing strategies that maximize GPU utilization while honoring each team’s allocation when it matters most. This post shows how quota management works, including how to configure quota shares with lending and borrowing strategies, set up in-share preemption for priority workloads, and get started using the SageMaker Python SDK. Administrators can allocate and share constrained GPU resources by defining a quota share for separate entities, such as individual teams or projects. Each quota share includes compute quotas (capacity limits) and resource-sharing strategies for idle compute. These strategies determine whether idle compute is reserved until jobs arrive ( RESERVE ), lent to other quota shares that have work available ( LEND ), or both lent when idle and borrowed when the share has work that might benefit ( LEND_AND_BORROW ). A quota share operates as a virtual queue nested hierarchically within an associated job queue. When scheduling jobs for a job queue, AWS Batch prioritizes quota shares that are under their capacity limits as it iterates through the associated quota shares. If jobs arrive in a quota share that has lent out its capacity, AWS Batch performs cross-share preemption. This reclaims resources for the lending quota share, so administrators don’t need to track down the jobs borrowing capacity and terminate them on their own. If jobs arrive in a quota share that is at or above its capacity limit, AWS Batch checks whether there’s available capacity to borrow from another quota share. If so, workloads can run using otherwise-idle capacity. You can turn on priority-based in-share preemption when you configure a quota share. Where cross-share preemption reclaims lent capacity as jobs arrive in a lending quota share, in-share preemption preempts lower priority jobs that are in the SCHEDULED, STARTING, or RUNNING state. This allows higher priority jobs at the front of the queue to start running sooner. Before you proceed with this example, you must have an AWS account with permissions to create and manage AWS Batch resources. For this example, see the sample IAM permissions needed to invoke AWS Batch and SageMaker APIs. The example uses the SageMaker Python SDK v3. Complete the setup required to install a compatible version of the SageMaker Python SDK: Using the new quota management capabilities requires creating a Scheduling Policy that contains a quotaSharePolicy , a Service Environment that specifies its capacity limits in terms of specific instances, and a SageMaker Training job queue that is connected to both. After that, you can associate quota shares to a job queue. The user guide has AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and console examples for configuring quota management resources and quota shares . An end-to-end example of quota management integrated with the aws_batch module in the SageMaker Python SDK v3 is contained in a sample notebook . In this example, we step through code snippets that summarize the key components, and use the helper functions from the notebook to create a Scheduling Policy, Service Environment, Job Queue, and three Quota Shares. The three quota shares configured here represent three different projects. Each has the same capacity limit set: a single ml.g5.xlarge instance. The QS1 quota share represents background jobs. For this project, you want to run the most important background job first and borrow as much spare capacity as is available. Within this quota share, no jobs are urgent, and preemptions are acceptable because all jobs use checkpointing. This quota share uses the LEND_AND_BORROW resource-sharing strategy and has in-share preemption turned on. Higher priority jobs within the same quota share can then preempt running jobs that are lower priority. QS2 represents medium priority workloads. Teams choosing this configuration would prefer to wait for capacity to become available rather than endure additional preemptions. Those preemptions come from borrowed capacity being reclaimed or from in-share preemptions because of higher priority job submission. This is appropriate for shorter jobs, or when most submitted jobs have similar priorities. The quota share still benefits from job priority being taken into consideration at job dispatch. Submitted jobs trigger AWS Batch to reclaim any lent capacity needed to run the jobs. QS3 represents workloads that need to start as quickly as possible with minimal interruptions. It’s configured to reserve capacity and neither lends nor borrows to other quota shares. It doesn’t experience cross-share preemptions, because its workloads don’t exceed their capacity limits. By also turning off in-share preemption, workloads submitted to this quota share are not preempted by AWS Batch as long as the capacity limit is unchanged. These quota share configurations are inputs to the create_quota_management_resources function in the sample notebook, which also configures the corresponding Scheduling Policy, Service Environment, and Job Queue with the constant names chosen. The aws_batch module within the SageMaker Python SDK has been extended to allow programmatic submission of SageMaker Training jobs to a quota-management-enabled AWS Batch job queue. To demonstrate these new capabilities, we use a Hello World ModelTrainer that’s submitted to the job queue. The following code snippet identifies an image URI to use based on the Region and instance type selected. We use this image URI within a basic hello world model trainer example: To use the job queue within the SageMaker Python SDK, provide the queue name to the TrainingQueue constructor within the aws_batch module. We can then submit three jobs to QS1, our background jobs quota share. The first job submitted has the highest priority, followed by the medium priority job, and then the lowest priority job. As nothing is currently running in QS1 or QS2, two instances’ worth of jobs should start, corresponding to the first and second jobs submitted (as they had the highest relative priority). Note that because this is only a hello world training job, it doesn’t require data, but typically a ModelTrainer requires data to perform training. The team that owns QS2 might discover they have work to perform and submit a job to QS2. Doing so triggers a preemption of capacity back from QS1, which is currently borrowing that capacity (QS3’s capacity isn’t configured to be borrowed). This is a cross-share preemption.

title: How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway
abstract: This post was co-written with Nikhil Kumar and Shakir Khan from MoEngage. When engineering teams start building AI agents, the capabilities those agents need usually already exist as internal APIs. Campaign creation, segment queries, delivery stats. The challenge isn’t building new functionality. The challenge is making hundreds of private APIs safely reachable by agents without exposing them to the public internet, without giving models control over identity, and without flooding context windows with hundreds of tool definitions. MoEngage, the agentic customer engagement platform that more than 1,350 consumer brands use to deliver personalized experiences across push, email, in-app, SMS, WhatsApp, and RCS, faced exactly this problem. Behind the product sit roughly 400 internal REST APIs, built by 25 engineering teams, running in private virtual private clouds (VPCs) across seven AWS Regions. MoEngage isolates these APIs regionally to meet data residency commitments and doesn’t expose them to the public internet. The capability the agents needed was already running in production. Making it reachable, safely, was the hard part. In this post, we walk through how MoEngage used AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to turn those private APIs into permission-scoped agent tools. The approach saved MoEngage an estimated six months of platform engineering effort, and onboarding a new API now takes hours instead of days. No product team wrote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server code, no networking was provisioned per integration, and no public endpoint exists anywhere in the path. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives agents a standard way to discover and call tools. The straightforward path to adopting it is for each team to expose its own MCP server. MoEngage costed that out and rejected it. Over 20 MCP servers means over 20 deployments to monitor, patch, and keep protocol-compatible as MCP evolves. Cross-domain agents, the useful ones that read a campaign, check its segment, and inspect delivery stats, would need to connect to several servers and reconcile them. And every team would need MCP expertise unrelated to its actual product work. So MoEngage established the principle that shaped everything that followed: Individual engineering teams do not implement MCP. Teams build REST APIs and declare which operations should be tools. The AI Platform team owns the MCP layer end to end. A team’s responsibility ends at a well-described OpenAPI spec. That principle immediately created three requirements: a central tool surface that agents connect to once rather than per-service, per-agent authorization enforced server-side rather than by convention, and private connectivity that does not need to be rebuilt for every new API. Building all of this from scratch was an option. A custom central MCP server would solve the 20-servers problem but leave MoEngage building a tool-generation pipeline, a policy file format, a tool-alias registry for renames, and circuit breakers. All custom code, all owned by one team, all of it undifferentiated work that does not make MoEngage’s agents smarter or its customers’ campaigns better. Before evaluating any solution, MoEngage defined four constraints. All four had to be met simultaneously. A solution that addressed two but broke the third and fourth was not viable. Nothing gets a public endpoint. MoEngage’s internal APIs are VPC-private by policy. Any solution that required exposing them, even behind additional authentication, was a non-starter. The conventional workaround is per-integration networking: a NAT gateway here, a reverse proxy there, a VPN tunnel for the third one. Multiply that by seven Regions and the operational surface grows faster than the set of agents does. Every new API would mean another networking change request, another set of security reviews, another piece of infrastructure to maintain. Identity can’t be an agent’s decision. Every internal API call carries tenant, user, role, and database context. If that context is a large language model (LLM)-visible tool parameter, a model can get it wrong or be talked into changing it. MoEngage needed identity to be structurally out of the model’s reach, injected by the calling service and not surfaced as something the model can set or override. A 400-tool catalog doesn’t fit in a context window. At roughly 50 tokens of JSON schema per tool, a full tools/list across the estate is over 20,000 tokens transmitted on every connection. That token budget is spent before the agent does anything useful, and it crowds out the context the agent actually needs to reason about the task. Client-side filtering ( tool_filter in ADK or the MCP SDK) doesn’t fix this. The full catalog has already crossed the wire, and filtering by client convention isn’t an authorization boundary. An agent that is not supposed to see write operations shouldn’t receive them in the first place. That last constraint is the one that avoided the obvious alternatives. A custom central MCP server solves the 20-servers problem but still leaves MoEngage building a tool-generation pipeline, a policy file format, a tool-alias registry for renames, and circuit breakers. All custom code, all owned by one team, none of it making MoEngage’s product better. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway is a fully managed MCP server. You register OpenAPI specs as targets and the gateway generates MCP tools from them, then routes calls to the backing services. Four properties mapped directly onto MoEngage’s constraints. OpenAPI in, MCP tools out. There’s no MCP server to build or operate, and no separate artifact to keep in sync with the API. The spec teams already maintain is the tool definition. Each operation becomes a tool named Target___operationId , for example CampaignsAPI___searchCampaigns . When the spec changes, the tool changes. When a team adds an endpoint, the tool appears. When a team removes one, the tool disappears. No deployment, no protocol expertise, no coordination with the AI Platform team. Cedar policies, evaluated before the catalog is serialized. The AgentCore policy engine uses partial evaluation to filter tools/list per principal. Each agent authenticates as its own IAM role, and its Cedar policy determines which tools it can see and call. This is what makes 400 tools tractable. It isn’t client-side filtering after the fact, but server-side scoping before the response is built. A campaign QA bot, for example, gets read access to campaign and segment tools but can’t call a write operation: The bot doesn’t see write tools in its tools/list response. There’s nothing to filter on the client side because the tools weren’t sent. Managed egress over Amazon VPC Lattice. The gateway reaches MoEngage’s internal services through AgentCore managed egress rather than through networking MoEngage builds and operates. Inbound, the gateway is reachable only through a VPC interface endpoint with private DNS. There’s no public path to it. Onboarding a new API adds a target, not a network topology change. This is the property that broke the multiply by seven Regions problem. The networking exists once and every API uses it. Semantic search as a gateway capability. With the x_amz_bedrock_agentcore_search capability, an agent can find tools by describing the task instead of naming the tool. It removed the need for a custom discovery layer. It also removed rename fragility as a side effect: if get_segment_user_count becomes get_segment_size , an agent searching for segment user count still finds it, because matching happens on description rather than identifier. The request flow from agent to internal API is short, and every layer has a specific job. Agent services connect through a VPC interface endpoint to AgentCore Gateway, which evaluates Cedar policies and routes tool calls through managed egress over Amazon VPC Lattice to internal APIs. The following diagram shows how the components connect.

title: Accelerate agentic AI with NVIDIA Nemotron models on Amazon EKS and SageMaker HyperPod EKS
abstract: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL joins the NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano , Nano Omni , Super , Ultra , and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning models already available on AWS. It’s a 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model that activates 12B parameters per token. It combines reasoning and tool use with text, image, document, and video understanding, so one model serves both text and visual tasks. This post explores its architecture and use cases, then shows how to deploy it on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) , Amazon EKS Auto Mode , and Amazon SageMaker HyperPod EKS . NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is an open multimodal model distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra. NVIDIA publishes the weights, training datasets, and post-training recipes, so you can customize the model for domain-specific workloads and run it on infrastructure you control. Model details: NVIDIA reports 63.44 percent on Hermes Bench and 87.05 percent on LangChain agent evaluations, and 80.8 percent on the CharXiv chart-reasoning benchmark. ( technical report ) Nemotron 3.5 Super VL uses a hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE architecture, interleaving Mamba-2, attention, and expert layers. Sparse routing activates 12B of the 120B parameters per token, so compute per token matches a much smaller model while GPU memory still holds the full weights. Mamba-2 layers carry a constant-size state during generation, so their memory does not grow with sequence length the way KV cache does, which keeps long contexts affordable. A recursively shared Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head supports native speculative decoding. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL supports agent workflows that combine reasoning with visual understanding: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL integrates with major open agent frameworks and orchestration systems through NVIDIA reference implementations, cookbooks, and the NVIDIA Agent Toolkit . For the full list of supported frameworks, see the NVIDIA developer blog . This section gives an overview of architecture, validation, and performance evaluation approaches. A detailed walkthrough of deploying Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Nemotron 3 Ultra on AWS is available in the aws-do-eks project, including prerequisites, cluster creation, model weights download, deployment, testing, benchmarking, and cleanup. The same pattern can also be applied to other models in the NVIDIA Nemotron family. The reference implementation runs on standard Amazon EKS, EKS Auto Mode, and SageMaker HyperPod EKS. With EKS Auto Mode, AWS manages scaling, GPU, and EFA support in the cluster on your behalf. The Kubernetes manifests for model deployment are the same for each of the orchestrator options. Each cluster has a control plane hosting the Kubernetes API and a data plane of CPU and GPU nodes. CPU nodes run system and test pods, while the GPU nodes run the model. Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) stores the container images, a shared Amazon FSx for Lustre volume holds the model weights, and Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) connects the GPU nodes. The following figure shows a standard Amazon EKS cluster. Figure 1: Standard Amazon EKS cluster architecture for serving NVIDIA Nemotron models NVIDIA Dynamo serves the model aggregated on a single node or disaggregated with prefill and decode on different nodes. For vision-language models, the image/video encoding stage can in addition run disaggregated on its own node. This architecture has been validated on both p6-b200.48xlarge (8 x NVIDIA B200 GPUs) and p5en.48xlarge (8 x NVIDIA H200 GPUs) instances. You can validate the cluster and its network with an NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) all-reduce micro-benchmark. Figure 2: GPU and EFA utilization during an NCCL all-reduce validation test Seeing utilization on all GPUs and traffic on all EFA adapters while the NCCL test is running, verifies that the cluster is working as expected. You can measure the performance of a deployed model on the cluster with the NVIDIA aiperf tool. Figure 3: aiperf performance metrics for the deployed model The aiperf output in the upper left pane shows key performance indicators (KPIs) like time to first token (TTFT), inter-token latency (ITL), and throughput in tokens per second (TPS). By taking these measurements at various levels of concurrency, we can study how latency and throughput depend on the number of concurrent requests. This information is essential to thoughtfully plan capacity and model deployment topology. The aws-do-eks container provides automation for visualizing GPU and EFA utilization as well as running aiperf and concurrency sweeps with single commands. Figure 4: Concurrency sweep comparing aggregated and disaggregated deployments The preceding concurrency sweep diagram reveals that the inference of Nemotron 3.5 Super VL has lower TTFT and about the same ITL between aggregated and disaggregated deployments on two nodes. A chart like this is useful when making deployment decisions. Draw your latency budget as horizontal lines, for example TTFT under 600 ms (about 1 second) and ITL under 100 ms per token. The rightmost point under both lines is the throughput one replica of this topology can serve within the service level objective (SLO), here c32, or about 320 tokens per second. To plan capacity, divide your target tokens per second by this per-replica throughput and find the number of prefill-decode pairs to deploy. Re-running the same sweep after a change (precision, TP/PP shape, aggregated versus disaggregated, a new Dynamo or vLLM release) makes the trade-off visible immediately. A curve that moves right and down is a win. Because TTFT and ITL are plotted separately, it also tells you which side to scale: rising ITL says add decode capacity, and rising TTFT says add prefill capacity. This post covers the architecture and performance evaluation patterns for serving NVIDIA Nemotron models on Amazon EKS, EKS Auto Mode, and SageMaker HyperPod EKS with NVIDIA Dynamo and vLLM. To get started, deploy Nemotron 3.5 Super VL in your own account, using the reference implementation . More inference blueprints are also available in the AI on EKS project. To get further hands-on experience with inference on EKS, register for our upcoming workshops . The authors would like to convey special thanks to everyone involved in developing, validating, reviewing, and publishing this content, including but not limited to: Eliuth Triana, Jiahong Liu, Kshitiz Gupta, Abhijeet Patil, Mike Stefaniak, Chris Splinter, Sheetal Joshi, Aditya Ramakrishnan, Natarajan Kumar, Anish Maddipoti.

title: What I learned about power from LBJ and Robert Moses
abstract: Thanks to Max Farrens , who paired with me in writing the script for this video essay. I recently interviewed Robert Caro. He’s spent the last 50 years writing a four volume biography of Lyndon Johnson, and he spent another 7 years before that writing the biography of Robert Moses, the master builder of New York. His books are widely regarded as the best explorations of political power that have ever been written. They also happen to be literally my favorite books ever. Whenever I meet somebody new, one of the first questions they ask me is, “Who is it that you most want to interview that you haven’t yet?” And for six years, I’ve answered the question the same way: Robert Caro. I’ve spent so much time trying to make this interview happen: chasing his agent, calling his publisher, contacting the museums that have his archives, and even sending him handwritten letters. I finally got to sit down with him, and I’m very happy with how it turned out. It’ll be out this Friday. In the meantime, as I was preparing for the interview, and rereading these biographies, I wrote down the lessons they laid out about how to accumulate and use power. Robert Moses was the master builder of New York. He built more of the physical city than anyone before or since: the Triborough and Verrazano bridges, the Cross Bronx Expressway, Jones Beach, Lincoln Center, Shea Stadium, two giant power dams upstate, in addition to hundreds of parks and dozens of pools. Of the 899 miles of highways completed in New York State by 1964, Moses had built 672 of them. His projects collectively cost hundreds of billions of dollars in today’s money. For more than 30 years, Robert Moses was the most powerful person in New York (more powerful than any elected mayor or governor, despite not being elected to anything). How did he get and keep that much power? Part of the answer is that Moses wrote the laws that governed him. He was called ‘the best bill drafter in Albany,’ and he used that skill to write himself powers that the legislators voting on his bills didn’t know they were granting. The political genius of Robert Moses is perhaps best illustrated by his use of public authorities, which are government-created corporations that build city infrastructure. Public authorities sell bonds to pay for a specific project, say a new bridge. Once the bridge is built, the authority would charge drivers a toll until it had collected enough money to pay off its bonds. Then the authority would tear down the tollbooths, hand the bridge over to the city, and go out of existence. At least, that was the idea. And that’s what Albany assumed would happen when the New York State Legislature approved the Triborough Bridge Authority Act of 1933, whose final version included - buried within pages and pages of legalese - a few seemingly minor alterations drafted by Robert Moses. Section 1 clearly stated that the authority would dissolve once the bonds were paid off. And since the bonds could run at most 40 years (and the revenues from the bridge would pay back the initial cost far sooner), it seemed like the authority had a clear, built-in expiration date. However, in a subsection of Section 9, Moses added a single sentence that said the Authority could “from time to time” pay off its old bonds by issuing new ones. And those new ones could be “for any other corporate purpose.” So just before the original bonds were about to expire, the authority now had the right to issue a totally fresh 40 year note, for a potentially totally different use. And what could the Authority build with all that money? The original act let it build two bridges and their “approaches.” Moses’ amendments also gave this authority the right to build “connecting” roads and “facilities not inconsistent with the use of the project”. These rights, when interpreted as creatively as Moses intended to, would allow Moses to alter most of the roads, parks, and housing in New York - for if a road connected to a road which connected to a road which connected to the bridge, or if a park lay along the road that connected to the road that connected to the road that connected to the bridge, surely the Triborough Authority was entitled to improve and change it. All this construction could be financed by the bridges’ enormous toll revenues and the right of the Triborough Authority to borrow against them. To give some perspective, in 1946, the entire New York City government could only borrow $150 million before hitting its legal debt limit. That very same year, Triborough could borrow $360 million. So Moses’ bridge authority had access to more than double the amount of money as the largest city in America. But what if a future governor or mayor eventually learned about all the power and revenue that had been delegated to this authority, and decided to claw back? Moses had planned for that too, and his solution was so clever that no lawyer or lawmaker in Albany saw it coming. The US Constitution says that no state shall make “any … Law impairing the Obligation of Contracts” entered into by a government entity. A bond issued by a public authority is such a contract. Moses snuck a clause into the law that allowed him to add into those bond contracts “any other matters, of like or different character, which in any way affect the security or protection of the bonds”. These “matters” included whether Triborough could charge tolls for however long they wanted, and whether they would get to keep the surplus thus generated. That is to say, Moses could now entrench his powers simply by writing them into the bonds he issued. From the moment the bonds were sold, those powers could no longer be revoked by the Legislature, the governor, or the mayor - by anything, in fact, short of a Constitutional Convention. The powers that Moses now had were guaranteed for the bonds’ entire lifetime - a lifetime which could always be extended simply by refinancing. So, with just a few minor tweaks, Moses turned an act meant to allow the construction of two bridges into the basis of an institution that could build basically anything it wanted anywhere in New York (and whose authority to do so was protected by the U.S. Constitution). These bond covenants had turned Triborough Authorities’ power into granite, but nothing in them guaranteed that Robert Moses would remain as chairman. So how did Moses retain his position for 30 years? Part of the answer is, again, the law. Moses drafted the Triborough act so that its commissioners could be removed mid-term only “on stated charges after a formal hearing.” But any differences he had with a mayor or governor were more about what he decided to build and whom he displaced to build it, rather than personal conduct. As Caro says, “Robert Moses was not himself corrupt. He was, in fact, as uninterested in obtaining payoffs for himself as any public servant who ever lived. In the politicians’ phrase, he was ‘money honest.’” So, there were never any formal charges to bring. But this only explains why he wasn’t fired in the middle of his term. Why was he reappointed every six years? Well, at his peak, Moses was a hydra with a dozen heads. He held 12 different government posts at the same time: city construction coordinator, chairman of the State Council of Parks, chairman of the State Power Authority, and so on. Some of these positions were appointed by the mayor, some by the governor, so no single person could cut off all his heads simultaneously. And removing him from any one position meant making an enemy of the man who would still be the most powerful person in New York. More importantly, no mayor or governor wanted to fire him. The way we remember Robert Moses today is based on a reputation that calcified in the 1970s, when The Power Broker came out and New York was experiencing a dark age of crime, deindustrialization, and white flight. Moses got much of the blame (the subtitle of The Power Broker is “Robert Moses and the Fall of New York”).

title: 文遠知行001號員工帶隊，景爍科技首輪融資數千萬美元
abstract: 文遠知行001號員工帶隊，景爍科技首輪融資數千萬美元 量子位的朋友們 2026-10-29 11:27:50 來源： 量子位 10月29日，文遠知行披露旗下子公司景爍科技首次融資進展 10月29日，文遠知行（NASDAQ: WRD，HKEX: 0800）披露旗下子公司景爍科技首次融資進展，景爍科技目前已獲嘉御資本、HKSTP香港科技園、天狼星資本等資方數千萬美元的pre-A輪共同投資。 景爍科技致力於構建物理AI時代的資料與模型基礎設施，以“高質量資料驅動物理AI進化”為核心理念，依託資料—模型一體化平臺WorldEngine和自研世界模型GENESIS-Robotics，形成覆蓋自研第一視角高精度資料採集裝置EGOK、規模化數採、高質量資料集與定製資料服務的產品體系，連線真實世界操作經驗與機器人學習過程。 目前，景爍科技已與全球數十家世界頂尖大模型公司和具身智慧企業建立合作，擁有100+客戶與生態合作夥伴，在手訂單金額數十億元，為物理AI和通用大模型研發與應用提供有力的資料支撐，年收入增長超100%，展現出強勁的商業化能力與增長潛力。 隨著人工智慧從數字世界加速邁向物理世界，高質量資料及相關基礎設施正成為推動技術演進和產業發展的關鍵要素。行業普遍認為，無論是大語言模型、世界模型還是具身智慧系統，其能力提升都建立在高質量資料的持續積累、治理和迭代之上。尤其在物理AI領域，真實世界資料的採集、處理、驗證和訓練已成為決定模型能力邊界的重要基礎。 作為文遠知行旗下業務之一，景爍科技依託文遠知行近十年的物理AI商業化落地經驗，持續強化世界模型、資料平臺及技能資產引擎能力，構建覆蓋資料生產、資料治理、模型訓練及能力沉澱的完整基礎設施體系，為下一代物理AI系統提供底層支撐。 景爍科技核心團隊來自文遠知行的物理AI研發體系，CEO霍達是文遠知行001號員工，長期深耕自動駕駛平臺與物理AI資料基礎設施建設，曾在美國、中國、新加坡主導全球化工程研發團隊搭建，具備豐富的技術架構與資料體系建設經驗。 本輪融資後，景爍科技將進一步擴充核心研發團隊，深化資料平臺、世界模型與技能資產引擎的協同能力，同時豐富高質量資料集的任務與場景覆蓋，加快面向物理AI領域的基礎設施能力建設。 從全球範圍看，當前AI產業快速發展，資料基礎設施企業持續受到資本市場青睞。2025年6月，美國科技巨頭Meta以143億美元戰略入股AI資料平臺Scale AI，對應公司估值達290億美元；同年10月，Mercor宣佈完成3.5億美元C輪融資，估值達100億美元；今年9月，Snorkel AI完成3.5億美元E輪融資，估值達35億美元。國內物理AI資料企業光輪智慧估值已達20億美元，並於今年6月完成新一輪10億元戰略融資。 本文由景爍科技提供，量子位獲授權轉載，觀點歸原作者所有。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 景爍科技 量子位的朋友們 STEPX Neo 釋出兩週即迎首次升級，智慧體能力持續釋放 2026-10-29 中國MaaS市場TOP2，商湯大裝置再度蟬聯 2026-10-29 AI安全是AI規模化應用“加速器” 2026-10-29 IDC最新報告：MaaS市場分化，PPIO拿下獨立服務商首位 2026-10-29

title: 小雨智造與國家鋼結構質檢中心共建實驗室，喬忠良：具身智慧新質生產力已成事實
abstract: 小雨智造與國家鋼結構質檢中心共建實驗室，喬忠良：具身智慧新質生產力已成事實 量子位的朋友們 2026-10-29 10:51:45 來源： 量子位 2026年10月27日，“工業具身智慧焊接與檢測技術聯合實驗室”正式揭牌成立。 2026年10月27日，由中冶建築研究總院有限公司國家鋼結構質量檢驗檢測中心與北京小雨智造科技有限公司共建的“工業具身智慧焊接與檢測技術聯合實驗室”正式揭牌成立。中國鋼結構協會會長、中國五礦集團首席科學家曾濱，中冶建築研究總院有限公司黨委書記、總經理王海濤，中冶檢測認證有限公司黨委書記、董事長劉冬，小雨智造創始人、CEO喬忠良共同為實驗室揭牌。儀式上，喬忠良發表致辭，並與劉冬共同向世界技能大賽焊接專案中國國家隊總教練周樹春、第48屆世界技能大賽焊接專案金牌獲得者趙錢森頒發了實驗室專家委員聘書，並透露了公司的首個客戶案例。 （實驗室揭牌成立） “具身智慧發展迅速，但越是在這樣的時刻，越需要守住質量這條底線。”喬忠良在致辭中表示，焊接不是一道普通的工序，每一道焊縫都關係著工程安全和人的生命。機器人可以把焊縫焊得更快，但如果質量不過關，效率越高，風險就越大。中冶建築研究總院有限公司國家鋼結構質量檢驗檢測中心是我國鋼結構領域唯一的國家級質檢中心，其焊接團隊主編《鋼結構焊接規範》等百餘項標準，培養出中國首枚世賽焊接金牌得主。喬忠良坦言，與這樣的“國家隊”同行，就是要做一件行業裡少有的事：把智慧裝備的工藝研發，與國家級權威質量驗證，在同一個平臺上徹底打通。“從今往後，具身焊接不僅要提升效率，質量也要更上一層樓——每一道焊縫，都要可檢驗、可溯源，經得起最嚴苛標尺的丈量。” 喬忠良透露，就在10月26日，小雨智造公佈了首個客戶案例：在老牌國企北泡輕鋼的一個車間裡，12臺小雨未來機器人已經進入日常作業。按2026年8月的資料，該車間月產能較改造前提升30%，同等焊接質量條件下綜合成本降低49%，單機日均產出約90米等效平角焊縫。“具身智慧帶來的新質生產力，不再是一個待論證的命題，而是一個已經發生的事實。”他進一步表示，具身智慧進工廠，接過了危險、艱苦、重複的工作，讓人站到了更有尊嚴的位置上。 （小雨智造創始人、CEO 喬忠良） 成立儀式上，世界技能大賽焊接專案中國國家隊總教練周樹春、第48屆世界技能大賽焊接專案金牌獲得者趙錢森受聘為實驗室專家委員。帶出四屆世賽冠軍的周樹春表示：“匠心不變，變的是手裡的工具。中國焊工焊接世界，下一代焊工，要帶著中國的機器人再去焊一次世界。”今年9月，趙錢森在上海舉辦的第48屆世界技能大賽上以世賽有史以來最高分一舉奪金，為中國捧回世賽焊接專案第4金。這位新科金牌獲得者則表示：“前輩把接力棒傳到我們手上，我們要發揚光大，拿下具身時代焊接技藝的金牌。”喬忠良表示，小雨智造邀請大國工匠加盟，是要讓匠心、技藝和經驗，沉澱為可傳承的工藝基座，再依託實驗室培養新一代既懂工藝、更懂AI的焊工。“實驗室連線的，是中國焊接工藝幾十年的深厚積澱，與人工智慧的澎湃未來。” （趙錢森） （周樹春） 公開資料表明，小雨智造成立於2023年，致力於打造“一腦多形”的通用機器人大腦及工業應用產品，願景是成為全球領先的通用智慧機器人平臺，讓智慧勞動力成為基礎設施，人人可享、無處不在。2026年7月，公司釋出首個產品小雨未來機器人，搭載輝達Orin算力平臺與梅卡曼德3D相機，絕對定位精度做到0.5毫米，通過自研的空間定位筆實現“一劃即焊”、免示教操作。 （聯合實驗室實景演示） 工業具身智慧焊接與檢測技術聯合實驗室的成立，標誌著國家級權威檢測能力與工業具身智慧前沿技術的深度融合。實驗室將以鋼結構國家級檢測標準為剛性標尺，開展具身智慧機器人焊接工藝開發、試樣檢測與效能驗證，同時面向鋼結構行業培養智慧焊接複合型人才，讓具身智慧焊接真正做到安全、穩定、精準、可靠和全程可檢驗，為中國鋼結構行業的智慧化升級、為發展新質生產力貢獻力量。這也意味著從客戶車間產線的資料驗證，到國家級檢測平臺的標準築基，工業具身智慧焊接正在完成從“前沿技術概念”到“工業級基礎設施”的關鍵一躍。 本文由小雨智造提供，量子位獲授權轉載，觀點歸原作者所有。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 小雨智造 量子位的朋友們 文遠知行001號員工帶隊，景爍科技首輪融資數千萬美元 2026-10-29 STEPX Neo 釋出兩週即迎首次升級，智慧體能力持續釋放 2026-10-29 中國MaaS市場TOP2，商湯大裝置再度蟬聯 2026-10-29 AI安全是AI規模化應用“加速器” 2026-10-29 相關閱讀

title: 剛剛，擴散模型殺進Agent主場！350億參數，速度比Jev快一倍
abstract: 剛剛，擴散模型殺進Agent主場！350億參數，速度比Jev快一倍 henry 2026-10-29 10:18:28 來源： 量子位 用擴散模型怎麼做做Agent？ henry 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 服了！天天在AI一線衝浪，竟然也會跟不上版本。 誰能想到，印象中用來生圖、生影片的 “擴散模型” ，竟然也能寫程式碼、生成網頁、呼叫工具，當Agent了！ 就在剛剛， 擴散智慧 釋出了全新的 擴散語言模型 —— Clover-35B-A3B-Preview 。 雖然名字裡多了“擴散”兩個字，但實際體驗下來，無論是寫程式碼、操作網頁、呼叫工具，還是生成HTML，用法都和我們熟悉的大語言模型差不多。 我個人用下來的第一感受就是一個字：“快”。 比如，讓它生成一個太陽系模擬器，Clover就思考了約1秒，然後也就4-5秒，一個能互動的太陽系模擬器就出來了。 再比如，我給它丟了一堆簡歷資訊，讓它整理成LaTeX格式的簡歷程式碼，也就十來秒，搞定～ 有一說一，用過GPT的朋友，應該都懂盯著“正在思考”等半天是什麼感覺，要不然最近也不會有主打快速決策的Jev什麼事兒～ 而說到Jev，Clover這次還真和它比了一把速度。 在網頁Agent評測WindTunnel的49個任務中，每個任務嘗試3次，Clover的中位執行時間為 1.52秒 ，Jev＋Mercury 2.5組合為 3.21秒 ，用時少了一半多。 嘗試成功率也略高，分別為 98.6%和95.9% 。 對比同表中的Gemini，速度更是快了好幾倍！ 好好好，你個擴散模型，要把自迴歸逼瘋？（doge） 會做Agent任務的擴散模型 說回模型，Clover-35B-A3B-Preview這次採用MoE架構，總參數350億，每個token啟用約30億參數，支援思考模式。 它進一步將團隊的擴散語言模型，從此前Dream 7B的 70億 參數，推進到了 350億 總參數規模。 更關鍵的是，參數量上來後，Clover的速度並沒有因此變慢，它在同尺寸對比中超過自迴歸模型。 除了前面的互動頁面和程式碼生成，官方演示裡，Clover還進一步展示了複雜任務、WebUI生成等Agent能力。 Clover可以通過WebMCP，連續處理六項任務，涉及開票、課程報名、金額彙總、活動狀態查詢、以及客戶資訊查詢和發票資訊查詢。 從下面的對比影片我們可以看出，Clover不僅成功完成任務，還在執行速度上徹底甩開了Gemini 3.6 Flash。 在線上購物場景中，Clover還能按要求找到指定款式、黑色、L碼的T恤，加入購物車，填寫訪客資訊，再走完測試結賬流程。 老實說，這種連續任務的處理其實是這次演示值得關注的地方。 要知道，擴散語言模型雖然有並行生成的速度潛力，但在做Agent任務時，以往的表現其實還不夠穩定： 模型工具呼叫格式可能出錯，也容易在同一個步驟上反覆嘗試，沒能根據返回結果調整動作。 Clover這次的進步，就體現在這些連續操作裡：呼叫工具、讀取反饋、繼續執行，直到完成任務。 具體到Benchmark，按照團隊公佈的資料，Clover在工具使用相關的τ³ Overall和BFCL-v4評測中，分別拿到65.3和67.9，位居前列。 △圖源：擴散智慧 Agent任務看完，再看看程式碼。 我又讓Clover生成了一個個人Agent的網頁介面。看起來也是有模有樣，整個生成過程也就十幾秒。 在程式碼評測這邊，Clover也交出了一組不錯的成績。 在考察真實程式碼倉庫問題解決能力的SWE-bench Verified上，它拿到 73.6 ；在考察終端任務執行能力的Terminal-Bench 2.1上，拿到 51.7 。 △圖源：擴散智慧 可以說，從生成互動頁面，到呼叫工具、跑完業務流程，再到程式碼評測，身為擴散語言模型的Clover，這次確實接了不少Agent的活。 哎，這就有意思了。印象裡負責去噪生圖的擴散思路，到了語言模型裡，究竟是怎麼生成文字、寫出程式碼的？ 難不成上面的demo真是AIGC出來的？ 擴散語言模型，什麼來頭？ 一般來說，我們熟悉的自迴歸（Autoregressive，AR）語言模型是根據前文預測下一個token，生成一個，再接著生成下一個，也就是大家常說的“詞語接龍”。 這裡的token，可以簡單理解成模型處理的文字片段。 相比於自迴歸模型的逐個序列預測生成，擴散語言模型則換了一種生成方式： 允許多個位置同時更新，再經過幾輪完善，逐步得到結果。 △圖源：AI生成 這裡的擴散去噪，可以理解為把被遮住或受到擾動的內容，逐步恢復成符合上下文的文字。 具體到Clover，它採用的是塊擴散：把待生成的內容分成若干塊， 塊與塊依次推進，塊內多個位置並行更新、相互參考。 這樣一來，一輪計算就有機會推動多個位置的生成，減少逐個生成帶來的等待。 但問題在於，能一起生成並不代表一輪就能寫好。 因為擴散模型往往需要多輪去噪，才能把結果逐步確定下來。輪數太少，內容可能還沒調整好；多來幾輪，計算開銷也跟著增加。 到了程式碼和Agent任務，上下文還會不斷變長。之前的要求、已經執行的操作、工具返回的結果，都可能影響下一步，歷史資訊的儲存和讀取也成了效率問題。 Clover的改進思路，就是讓歷史記憶和當前生成各司其職。 它圍繞塊擴散重構了門控Delta網路（GDN）：已經生成的上下文被壓縮排持續更新的狀態，供後續步驟讀取；當前生成的塊則通過雙向注意力，讓塊內的token相互參考。 與此同時，Clover將歷史記憶的讀出作為獨立的資訊單元，與當前token一起參與注意力計算，讓模型自己學習如何權衡前文與當前內容；再通過可學習的塊大小校準，減少塊變大後歷史資訊被稀釋的問題。 換句話說，這些調整的目標，就是讓並行生成、歷史資訊利用和計算效率更好地配合，這也是Clover將擴散語言模型進一步推進到程式碼和Agent任務的關鍵。 而除了Clover以外，擴散語言模型這兩年之所以受到關注，也主要在於它相對於自迴歸的兩大優勢： 一方面，擴散語言模型允許多個位置同時生成，有機會減少逐token生成帶來的序列等待。對於需要反覆生成程式碼、呼叫工具的Agent，這種潛力尤其值得關注。 另一方面，生成過程中，前後內容可以相互參考。在雙向建模的設計下，多個位置能在迭代中共同調整，為處理內容之間的依賴關係提供另一種方式。Clover當前塊內的互動，就是其中一種實現。 圍繞這些可能性，學術界和產業界已經給出了不同的嘗試。 何愷明今年參與的ELF，嘗試在連續嵌入空間中生成語言；谷歌推出的DiffusionGemma，探索並行文本生成；國內大廠也在研究面向程式碼任務的擴散語言模型。 具體方法各不相同，大家都在嘗試把另一種生成方式，變成能用起來的能力和效率。 Clover這次，則把自己的進展放進了程式碼、工具呼叫和連續任務裡，交給使用者上手檢驗。 從DiffuSeq到Clover，擴散智慧的下一步 最後，讓我們說回Clover背後的團隊—— 擴散智慧 。 據悉，擴散智慧由香港大學孔令鵬教授及其博士生龔珊三、葉佳成聯合創立。團隊成員對擴散語言模型的探索，可以追溯到2022年。 那一年，他們提出了DiffuSeq，研究如何用擴散模型完成序列到序列的文本生成：給定一段文字，再按條件生成另一段文字。 當時要邁過的一道坎，就是把擅長處理影像等連續訊號的擴散方法，用到離散的自然語言上。 到了2025年4月，團隊核心成員參與推出Dream 7B，將研究推進到70億參數語言模型。 根據當時公佈的結果，Dream 7B在通用、數學和程式碼任務上，取得與同規模自迴歸模型可比的表現，也展示了規劃能力和生成順序上的靈活性。 再到這次的Clover，模型規模繼續擴大，寫程式碼、呼叫工具、連續執行任務，都成了重點展示的內容。 這條路線，也就從最初研究怎麼生成文字，一步步走到了如何把複雜任務做對、做快。現在，團隊還在往多模態和端側延伸。 據介紹，Clover後續也將推出多模態版本，團隊正在推進擴散語言模型與多模態理解及動作生成的結合，並持續開展端側場景的適配與驗證。與Acrab的合作，則在推進面向端側場景的系統適配和軟硬體協同驗證。 按照團隊計劃，接下來還會繼續探索更大規模的模型，提高長程任務的穩定性，並通過推理最佳化、量化和部署適配，推進端側應用。 最後的最後，咱們不妨藉著這次新發布的Clover開個腦洞： 人類思考時，究竟是一句接一句往下推，還是先有個模糊的整體，再逐漸補全細節—— 大腦究竟更像自迴歸，還是擴散？ 體驗連結 [1]https://diffuspace.ai/register 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 Agent 擴散模型 henry 剛剛，Gemini 4終於來了：谷歌重回御三家，API限時半價 2026-10-16
