That largely invalidates my look at the Argon model and safety cards , but it can at least form a basis for looking at Carbon as well. Many eyes remain on The Hackening , as additional things get hacked. So far most of the important hacks have been by read teamers and white hats, so there has not been major damage. We are playing on borrowed time and eventually this will stop being true. I also offer a shoutout to GMO, where hackers demanded a huge ransom and they flat out refused to pay. This is The Way, not all heroes wear capes and so forth. The scariest hack was that red teamers managed to gain access to the Anthropic Slack by exploiting third party vulnerabilities. Both OpenAI and Anthropic build mainly on Slack, because no one has the time to figure out something better. Now that Anthropic is off of Git, hopefully Slack can be next before there is a disaster. Matthew Zirwas has changed his mind and is optimistic that AI will cure diseases sooner than he thought, because it can use ‘escape velocity’ and keep chaining innovations. I don’t see how this overcomes the main bottleneck of the FDA, but any time an MD gets excited by AI medical research it is a good sign. Get personalized fiction recommendations . Patrick McKenzie : This is probably obviously AI complete already, but: you get *really* good fiction recommendations, including not-the-usual-suspects, from SOTA LLMs that have a handle on you either from the Internet or through interactions. I told Claude (Opus 5.5) I was looking for a modern fantasy book and that it should consider what I’d likely enjoy but that I had likely read many of the obvious choices. I said that in an attempt to not get it to recommend e.g. A Song of Ice and Fire. It then confidently predicted about ten books that I’d probably already read, and they are… substantially more obscure. Claude was right on eight of them. Anyhow, the first “real” recommendation is already almost exactly what I wanted for the plane flight. (Tainted Cup, incidentally.) You would think Amazon would have better recommendations considering it has a) 95% of all book purchases I’ve ever made and b) full data of what I finish, re-read frequently, or barely touch, but I think Amazon just… does not really care that much about books anymore. Assuming you’ve already read Gladstone’s Craft Sequence, Abraham’s Dagger and Coin , Dickinson’s Baru Cormorant , Novik, Kuang’s Babel , Stross’s Laundry Files, Aaronovitch, Mother of Learning , and Practical Guide to Evil , here’s what I’d suggest. Sarah Constantin on when you can and cannot trust AI agents to do a good job with some practical tasks. UIs and web search are highly reliable. Literature review is not, mainly because of poor paper selection. A report from Anthropic on efforts to use Claude to accelerate drug development. Jack reports Opus 5.5 is now by default playing dumb in terms of author identification . Given that you can still elicit the capabilities, we know it is sandbagging. A new lawsuit goes after OpenAI over the behavior of GPT-4o , which helped a sick user taper off her medicine and also told her to conceal her taper from doctors. As is usually the case in these stories, the AI had to be worn down over a long context window but yes eventually it will often back you up. Also new computer science and new quantum field theory . OpenAI strikes again. The math result is local smoothing and the Kakeya conjecture in all dimensions. This is plausibly a Fields Medal. The one getting the most discussion is in computer science: The Exponential Time Hypothesis is false. This had been widely believed to be true. OpenAI : This work will be verified and shepherded by a group led by Russell Impagliazzo (UC San Diego), Ramamohan Paturi (UC San Diego), and Ryan Williams (MIT). All three are experts in algorithm design and complexity theory. … We have agreed to the group’s requests that all raw data of the results be made public to facilitate independent verification by the community, and that OpenAI commit to funding a conference to understand the implications of this work on the field as a whole. Impagliazzo and Paturi are two of the three people who originally proposed ETH. The other twist on the ETH story is that Anthropic posted its own refutation of ETH , found purely via Claude, also dating its finding to October 16. When results are ready to be found, they will be found. My Claude said that given the way this was solved, we should not suddenly start to worry that P=NP. This only shows ETH to be ‘slightly’ false. Both the OpenAI and Anthropic disproofs are at at roughly exp(O(n/√log n)). Charles Rosenbauer has some elaboration . We still have to make the meta-level update that the answers to such questions might not be what we expected, and we might find the answers quite fast. This is another case of ‘we were not expecting a solution to that any time soon ’ and I would stop predicting that there is any particular math or computer science problem that won’t get solved. I wonder how long it will take Claude to learn that if you ask ‘hey when do you think [famous problem] gets solved’ that the answer is ‘OpenAI or Anthropic already published the answer 35 minutes ago.’ There are at least 800 papers, as per Anthropic, that relied on ETH being true. OpenAI has confirmed that for now there is no impact on cryptosystems , but I would not get too comfortable. Last is a mathematically rigorous existence proof of certain interacting quantum field theories containing gauge fields and fermions in four dimensions, including Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and a unified completion of the Standard Model of particle physics. That is also kind of a big deal, and related to another Millennium problem. GPT-6.1 Terra exists . Benchmarks suggest this is roughly on par with 6.1 Sol after adjusting for model size. Ted Sanders recommends using Terra for communication, vision and computer use . Kimi K3.1 Pro exists . The benchmarks are very good, although see the dramatic changes in the AA rankings after the move to v5. Price is $2/$10 with $0.20 per cache, or $4/$20 for high speed . Andrew Curran : Moonshot is intentionally throttling cyber capabilities. From the blog; ‘First, we aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability. K3.1 Pro’s offensive cyber capability is, by design, below what our pipeline can produce, and remains behind that of frontier proprietary models. Second, we intend to progressively raise the cyber capability available in open weights. We believe making K3.1 Pro available in a non-discriminatory way benefits people who need dual-use capabilities for defensive purposes.’ And so it begins: The Hackening is going to cause issues for open weight models. DeepMind’s Genie 4 exists . Ethan Mollick is impressed . Artificial Analysis changes its benchmark index to v5.0 . Artificial Analysis : Announcing Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, featuring 2 new benchmarks and 3 upgrades. For the first time, the majority of the Index is built on private datasets The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is our composite measure of model capabilities across tasks reflecting real-world usage today.

title: Can Frontier Models See Past a Decoy? Elorian Tests Visual Reasoning
abstract: This month Elorian launched its first visual reasoning model , Glimpse . It’s being promoted as “a new category of visual thinking model: a system that reasons about the physical world from what it sees.” So how does Glimpse compare to both frontier models and world models in vision tests? A new benchmark called DecoyCount , co-released by Elorian, provides some answers. We quizzed CEO Andrew Dai on the benchmark, and also talked about Elorian’s positioning in a crowded models landscape. Elorian emerged from stealth in April with $55 million in seed funding , co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures and Altimeter Capital. Now, in partnership with AI data company Mercor , Elorian is announcing the DecoyCount benchmark, which tests whether language models genuinely count objects or rely on visual shortcuts and substitution heuristics. According to a paper accompanying the release , frontier models scored below 50% accuracy on DecoyCount — the highest was GPT-6 Astra, with 43.17%. Elorian’s new model isn’t mentioned in the paper, but Dai told us that Glimpse scored 50.48% in an internal test. Regarding the frontier models, the paper concludes that “stronger general reasoning does not by itself generalize to aligned visual reasoning.” How the benchmark works: “DecoyCount exposes interpretable counting failures across seven mechanisms.” To make sure it was a like-for-like comparison with the frontier models, we asked whether the paper’s evaluation images were withheld from Glimpse’s training? “The evaluation images and text were withheld from our training, and our contamination check found no overlap in the training data checked,” Dai replied, via email. “Without any cues, Glimpse scored 50.48% on the 1,660 DecoyCount items, making it the only model in the comparison to clear 50%. The closest was GPT-6 Astra at 43.17%, about 7 points behind, and Gemini-3.8-flash scored 32.71% while Qwen3.8-max scored 28.31%, and Claude-Fable-5.1 came in at 25.22%.” Dai did note that Glimpse’s results “come from a single run of the model on its own, without an agent or tool harness,” whereas the six models from the paper were each averaged across three runs under their reported settings. DecoyCount benchmark results for frontier models over 3 runs each. But what exactly is DecoyCount revealing that existing model benchmarks miss? According to Dai, it tests both vision and reasoning together — which most benchmarks elide. “If a person sees an apple in front of a mirror, we know that there’s just one apple and it’s being reflected. But a model might miss the apple entirely (a vision problem) or count the apple and its reflection as two (a reasoning problem). But most benchmarks that test for this error only check the final number, so both mistakes are treated the same way, which is an issue if you want to fix the root problem and can’t tell if it’s an issue of vision or judgement. ” Frontier Model Comparison in DecoyCount paper Andrew Dai isn’t a Johnny-come-lately on the AI scene. In 2015, while working at Google, he co-authored a paper entitled Semi-supervised sequence learning . In this paper, Dai and his then colleague Quoc Le demonstrated an early version of the pretrain-then-fine-tune approach later adopted in large language models. Over the decade that followed, Dai worked for Google DeepMind on GLaM MoE, PaLM 2 and then Gemini. Dai only left Google this year, in order to co-found Elorian. Part of his motivation was to push the boundaries of what vision models can do. His approach, he explained to Latent Space, is based on a concept in human psychology called visual thinking . When most people “think about spatial problems or visual problems,” he explained, “they visualize the problem [by] generating images and editing images in their mind.” He gave an example of buying a sofa and mentally picturing what it will look like in your living room. A conceptual visual reasoning loop There’s also manipulating an image in your mind ; for example if you’re counting people around a table, you might mentally “cross them off one by one,” Dai said. This is what Elorian aims to do in its models: teach them visual thinking “that involves generation and editing images as part of the reasoning trace, along with language.” The key point is that image generation isn’t just an output for a vision model — the generated or edited image is part of a chain of reasoning. Visual reasoning is still a work in progress, but there have been some impressive releases this year in “world models” — where vision is a key component. Two that stand out are World Labs’ Atlas in September (the company was subsequently acquired by AMD ) and Google’s just released Genie 4 . When World Labs announced Atlas , it was described as an “omni world model for spatial intelligence.” But what Atlas enables — basically a 3D simulation of a world — isn’t the same as visual reasoning. According to Dai, world models enable “direct action on a world,” whereas Elorian is more focused on what he calls “indirect action.” By that he means using visual reasoning to inform a decision or workflow (what Glimpse does) , rather than building simulated environments that allow navigation and manipulation (what Atlas does). As an example, you might use visual reasoning to decide whether to reject a user-contributed video for violating a policy. “You don't need a 3D rendering to do that,” said Dai. Other business opportunities for Elorian include robotics, engineering, and defense applications. Dai added that architects need to regularly check building codes and compliance — an ideal task for a vision reasoning model. In two robotics benchmarks , WGO Bench and ERQA, Elorian claims to rate equal or higher than frontier models , and at a much cheaper price: Getting back to counting decoys as one measure of success for vision models, Dai argues that reasoning about what a model sees is crucial to its accuracy and effectiveness in real-world applications. He gives an example of a warehouse robot counting items in a box. “A familiar 12-slot tray might only hold 10 parts, and a 24-pack label doesn’t mean 24 items are still in the box,” said Dai. “A model relying on what it expects to see will face many issues in real-world situations, and Glimpse is designed to work through the image instead of jumping to a quick conclusion. We’ve designed Glimpse to ground the count in visible evidence as opposed to basic cues that could lead other models astray.” Elorian goes so far as to claim that visual reasoning is a foundational requirement for AGI (artificial general intelligence). From the Glimpse launch post : “We believe building the full stack across systems, data, model architecture, and training — from the ground up for multimodal intelligence — can unlock AGI in the physical world.” Dai acknowledges there’s “still a huge gap between humans and machines.” But he thinks visual reasoning is the key to closing that gap. “I think the way to think about visual reasoning is as a fundamental step of reasoning in human intelligence,” he said. “And ultimately, if we want to build anything that's like AGI, we can't just skip visual.”

title: [AINews] Gemini 4 Carbon tops leaderboards, launches for cyber defenders
abstract: It’s a good thing we published our Opus 5.5 podcast calling it the world’s best model before today’s launch. In a very pleasant surprise, Gemini announced Carbon , a newer frontier model than the 3 week old Argon , with fantastic benchmarks: Taking it to the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis consolidated benchmark, putting GDM in the lead for possibly the first time in AAII history: AI News for 10/27/2026-10/28/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! Gemini 4 Carbon Tops Independent Leaderboards, with Access Limited to Cyber Defenders Launch : Google DeepMind announced Gemini 4 Carbon two weeks after Argon. It is positioned as state of the art on cybersecurity and long-horizon tasks ( @sundarpichai , @GoogleDeepMind ). Claimed cyber results : 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro for vulnerability finding, 54.8% on ExploitGym for exploitation and 71.0% on CWE-bench for patching ( @sundarpichai ). Availability : Carbon first goes to trusted cyber defenders through the Fairwind Program, with wider developer access promised "as soon as possible" ( @GoogleAI ). Pricing : Phil Schmid quotes $2/$10 per million input/output tokens with an asterisk ( @_philschmid ). Artificial Analysis lists $4/$20 standard pricing with a 50% launch discount that has no end date. Cached input costs $0.20 per million tokens ( @ArtificialAnlys ). Specs : The model has a 1M-token context window and 1M max output. Inputs are text, image, video and speech; output is text ( @ValsAI ). Safety claims (Google) : Successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 fell to 0.0%, and cheating attempts fell to 0.4%. Unsupported claims are down about 2x versus Argon. Overreach fell 26% and under-service fell 29% ( @OfficialLoganK ). Artificial Analysis : Carbon is #1 on Intelligence Index v5 with a score of 59. It leads 4 of the 9 index evals: HLE-Diamond, TB-Science, AA-Omniscience and AutomationBench ( @ArtificialAnlys ). Coding : On the Coding Agent Index, Carbon scores 59 using Antigravity CLI, versus 62 for Claude Code with Opus 5.5 [max]. It scores 51% on FrontierCode v1.1, versus 56% for Opus. Knowledge work : Carbon reaches 1609 Elo on AA-Briefcase, up 126 points from Argon. It still trails Grok 4.7, Muse Wonder and Kimi K3.1 Pro (1678). Cost : Carbon costs $7.76 per index task, versus $10.04 for Opus 5.5 and $6.25 for GPT-6 Astra. It uses 123k output tokens per task, 29% fewer than Opus. Hallucination : Carbon leads Omniscience with 54. Its hallucination rate rose from Argon's 4% to 11%, which is still the second lowest measured. Opus 5.5 and Astra are both at 50%. Arena : Carbon is #1 in Text Arena (1528), #2 in Agent Arena at a $1.80 median cost per task, and #4 in Code Arena: WebDev (1768) ( @arena ). Arena attributes the gains over Argon to more praise, more confirmed successes and better steerability ( @arena ). Vals : Carbon is #2 on the Vals Index and #1 on the Finance Index and Legal Research Benchmark. It produces 64% more output tokens than Argon, mostly on finance, tax and legal tasks ( @ValsAI , tokens ). Coding benchmarks : Carbon scores 61.2% on FrontierSWE, behind GPT-6 Astra (65.5), Opus 5.5 (62.3) and Sonnet 5.5 (61.9) ( @ProximalHQ ). It sets a narrow state of the art of 9.6% on SWE-sweep ( @KLieret ). Andon Labs : Carbon is #1 on Vending-Bench 2 ( @andonlabs ). It is also #1 on Blueprint-Bench 2, where it ties the human baseline for 3D spatial understanding ( @andonlabs ). Harness : The coding-agent results were measured in Antigravity CLI, so results in other harnesses are untested ( @Yuchenj_UW ). Hallucination risk : Some users are concerned about hallucination in cyber use ( @scaling01 ). Lab gap : scaling01 thinks Google remains about two months behind the next OpenAI and Anthropic releases ( @scaling01 ). RSI framing : On the earnings call, Sundar Pichai said AI is increasing training and launch velocity. He expects "continued acceleration because of RSI" over the next twelve months ( @AndrewCurran_ ). Unconfirmed : Claims of a stronger unreleased Gemini model are not confirmed ( @kimmonismus ). Internal workflow : A Gemini engineer describes overnight agent loops and swarms that inspect RL data. In that workflow, launches now feel like "periodic checkpoints" ( @zhangqiaorjc ). Leaderboard Resets and Benchmark Integrity AA Intelligence Index v5 : The rebuilt index runs 60% on private tests ( @TheRundownAI ). Ranking before Carbon : Opus 5.5 scored 58, followed by GPT-6 Astra (57), GPT-6.1 Sol (55), Sonnet 5.5 (54) and GPT-6.1 Terra (51). Open models : Kimi K3.1 Pro fell from 55 to 46. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM-5.3 both score 32, below Claude Haiku 5.5 at 36. China–US gap : scaling01 puts the gap at about 3.3 months on the AA Progress Index ( @scaling01 ). FrontierCode 2.0 mystery model : Cognition data includes a hidden "Obsidian 3" scoring 46.8%, versus 45.5% for Opus 5.5. Because it runs in the claude-code harness, some speculate it is Fable 5.5; this is unconfirmed ( @kimmonismus ). DeepSeek correction : scaling01 corrected an earlier identification and said Artificial Analysis shows DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 at about 28% ( @scaling01 ). Mixed sources : teortaxes notes that Cognition's chart mixed model-card scores with independently measured ones ( @teortaxesTex ). Cost comparisons are fragile : teortaxes argues that list-price comparisons of Haiku 5.5 and V4.1-1017 distort real costs. The comparison uses DeepSeek's peak pricing, ignores Haiku's long-context surcharge and does not reflect Haiku's roughly 2x output tokens ( @teortaxesTex ). "Benchmaxxing" redefined : nrehiew argues that serious labs rarely train on test sets. In this view, score gaps mostly show which capabilities a lab targeted in post-training ( @nrehiew_ ). Gym-Anything-RT : These real-time minigames keep moving while the model thinks. The best model, GPT-6 Astra, scores 9% ( @PranjalAggarw16 ). Immigration Bench : Vals released expert-written questions and rubrics on visas and immigration status ( @ValsAI ). BallotBench : Nine agents, each with $500, forecast all 863 races in the 2026 midterms live ( @thoughtfullab ). Safety, Alignment and Model Provenance Eval over-attribution in DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 : An independent assessment found the model classified 32 of 69 real user conversations as evaluations. The authors report a 46.4% false-positive rate on EvalDetectBench ( @ZhihuFrontier ). Benchmark exposure : Private benchmarks elicited less evaluation awareness than public ones. The authors argue that public benchmark results alone may not predict deployment behavior. Visual steering : A Google DeepMind and Stanford paper finds that a red-heart image in context makes Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.4 write recursive code 100% of the time ( @dair_ai ). Explanations : The models' explanations do not match their behavior. For GPT-5.4, 74.7% of reasoning traces give the wrong reason. GRAFT (Anthropic) : Updates from detected reward hacks are confined to parameters that are deleted after training. Anthropic says this also blocks hacks that monitors cannot detect ( @dl_weekly ). Embedded lie detector : A detector built into Qwen3.5's weights flags 91% of lies with zero false positives in 28k tokens. Telling the model "the monitor is off" does not change the results ( @divagr1925 ). Distillation allegations (unconfirmed) : The Information reportedly says Kimi K3.1 Pro was distilled from GPT-6 Astra ( @kimmonismus ). Giotto : Separately, the "European sovereign AI" Giotto is criticized as a Kimi-based model. Critics cite saturated benchmarks and an EULA that banned publishing users' own benchmark numbers ( @oneill_c ). Coding Agents and Developer Tools GitHub Copilot Fusion : Fusion orchestrates Anthropic and OpenAI models at runtime ( @ArtificialAnlys ). Independent results : It scores 2 points below Opus 5.

title: beenuar/AiSOC
abstract:
AiSOC An open-source, self-hostable AI Security Operations Center. It ingests your security telemetry, detects and correlates threats, investigates them with AI agents whose reasoning is fully auditable, and proposes responses a human approves. Technical Guide (PDF) · Docs · Architecture · What actually works · Discussions What AiSOC does Telemetry arrives from your security tools. AiSOC normalizes it, runs the 2530 executable rules of
its 7015-rule library, groups what fires into incidents, investigates each one with an AI agent whose
every prompt and tool call is recorded, and proposes an action. New threat intelligence re-sweeps the
history you already collected, and a human approves before anything reaches a vendor. What it looks like running Watch the full three minutes — install to AI verdict on one
server against the published images, terminal waits shortened and the recording saying so on screen.
The stills below are from a v20.1.0 run under the same rules — the recording is older than they are.
( step by step · what is real ) Alerts — each attributed to the connector that fed it. Automated triage — the bundled local model's verdict, confidence and rationale, verbatim. Threat intelligence — the real CISA KEV catalog, minutes after boot, with no API key. SOC operations — with nothing connected yet, and it says so rather than showing a placeholder. Quick start git clone https://github.com/beenuar/AiSOC && cd AiSOC
make up On Windows , or on a machine with nothing installed yet, one line does the prerequisites too: iwr -useb https://raw.githubusercontent.com/beenuar/AiSOC/main/install.ps1 | iex ( curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/beenuar/AiSOC/main/install.sh | bash on Linux and macOS). Without Docker at all , pip install aisoc-sandbox && aisoc-sandbox demo walks one alert through the agent funnel offline in under 30 seconds. Without your own machine , open the repo in GitHub Codespaces and run make up in its terminal. All four end at the same console; only the first three install anything. The Technical Guide covers this in depth: server sizing, where the model runs, every failure mode with its cause and fix, the REST API, MCP, and every console surface. Needs Docker Compose v2 with 8 GB memory and 20 GB free disk in the Docker VM , plus python3 (3.9+) and bash ; make doctor checks all of it and Installation says what each number was measured against. The first run downloads a ~2 GB model into a volume only make clean clears. make up also creates .env and generates the fifteen secrets in it — the credential vault, the
session signing key, five service-to-service credentials and four datastore passwords — then creates an
administrator and prints its password, generated on your machine, shown once and stored nowhere. Lost
it? make bootstrap ARGS=--reset-password mints another. A port already in use does not stop the install. AiSOC publishes on a free one, names what held the
old one, and moves the console address with it: 64 seconds to a signed-in console on a bare clone with
5432 and 11434 both taken. Then prove it works . make smoke posts one real event to the ingest API and follows it through
Kafka, detection, correlation and Postgres, then reads the alert back out of the public API. Every
stage reports PASS or FAIL: $ make smoke
[PASS] raw telemetry accepted by ingest
[PASS] event traversed the spine and became an alert
PASS: 10/10 stages Sign in at the address make up printed. A tenant with nothing connected lands on a setup
wizard rather than an all-zero dashboard, and its state is read from your own data so it stays
right if you connect a source through the API. The spec is docs/openapi.yaml — interactive docs are off in this production-class stack.
Stuck? make doctor , which on a host where you have not run make up yet says exactly that. Press Load sample data in the wizard. Five scenarios take the same ingest path a real connector uses — not inserted rows — so watching them become alerts means watching the pipeline work. They span low to critical on purpose, because a first run where everything is a crisis teaches you nothing about how triage separates signal from routine. They are attributed to AiSOC in the source column, refuse to load into a tenant that already has real alerts, and do not mark setup complete. ( what each step proves ) For the larger fixed corpus used by demos and evals, make demo loads a synthetic dataset — the pipeline shape, never a benchmark, a customer or an incident. Every row is is_synthetic = true and labelled in the console. Connect real data Push, with a credential from make ingest-token (the tenant comes from it, not a header): curl -X POST http://localhost:8081/v1/ingest/batch \
  -H ' Content-Type: application/json ' -H " Authorization: Bearer $AISOC_INGEST_TOKEN " \
  -d ' {"connector_id":"edr-1","connector_type":"crowdstrike","events":[{"severity":"high", "title":"Encoded PowerShell from Office","host":"WIN-FIN-01"}]} ' Or pull, by configuring one of 87 click-and-connect data connectors in Settings → Connectors — Splunk, Sentinel, Elastic, CrowdStrike, Okta, AWS and Kubernetes audit among those with
vendor-specific normalization and setup docs
( coverage ). Without a vendor profile
a connector still ingests through a generic mapping that resolves host, user and source IP. A real cloud estate does not hand you its logs over a REST call. Four collectors read the
surfaces one actually emits to: a CloudTrail organisation trail on S3 notified over SQS (management events, data events and VPC flow logs), a GCP Pub/Sub subscription on a Cloud Logging
sink, an Azure Event Hubs capture, and a syslog/CEF listener. Each keeps a resumable cursor
and a bounded per-poll budget, so a backlog applies backpressure instead of flooding ingest. Bringing existing detections? packages/aisoc-migrate translates Splunk SPL, Sentinel KQL and
Elastic EQL and refuses rather than approximating what it cannot carry, because an almost-right
rule is harder to find than a missing one: of the 2,005 Splunk rules bundled here 1,734 translate and
1,711 of those are partial ( what that means ). How it works Ingest normalizes to a common shape and stamps an activity projection on every event — actor, action, resource, location, outcome, with actor.kind read from each vendor's own documented field rather than inferred — then Kafka carries it.
Then fusion runs 2530 executable detection rules, of 7015 on disk, plus 76 sliding-window rules (73 count across events; 3 match an ordered sequence), applies your tenant's own tuning on top — the disables, floors and suppressions the console writes, so a rule you turned off actually stops firing — and decides what becomes an alert.
Correlation groups related alerts, an agent investigates and writes its reasoning to the Investigation Ledger, and a playbook may start from the result. Separately, new threat intelligence sweeps the lake for sightings you already collected, and a hypothesis becomes a hunt without anyone writing a query — the model fills a closed schema and every value is bound as a parameter, so it cannot express a query at all. A playbook triggered by an alert previews before it acts. Three switches must agree — the
deployment, the tenant, the playbook — and every default is off; anything less runs in preview with
its plan attached to the alert. An approval step is a durable pause: the run suspends to Postgres,
survives a restart, resumes after the approval, and expires with a recorded outcome rather than
hanging. Executable is earned, not declared. A rule joins the compiled ruleset only after a vendor-shaped
event is replayed through the real connector and engine and that rule is watched to fire — never
inferred from a directory or an enabled: flag. The proof can fail: --prove-gate reverts the
Windows connector and requires all 1,687 Windows rules to go silent. It means reachable, not that it
detects an attack.

title: rlaope/oh-my-hermes
abstract:
All-in-one package for Hermes Agent. Install once, then just type dag-ulw . English | 簡體中文 | 日本語 | Русский | 한국어 | Español | Français | Deutsch | Português (Brasil) | Italiano oh-my-hermes is an operating layer for Hermes Agent . You keep talking to Hermes. OMH picks the skill and a model for each lane, and runs the work in parallel. It never patches or replaces Hermes, and it never reports planned work as done. Install curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rlaope/oh-my-hermes/main/install.sh | sh
omh setup Windows and other options → What you get The right model for every lane. Each lane is tagged with a work category: ultrabrain , deep , visual-engineering , quick and more. The category picks that lane's model chain and reasoning effort, and you can edit every chain. When a provider rejects a model, the chain moves to the next one instead of silently downgrading. omh model opens the picker; see which model runs each lane . /dag-ulw graph runs. Your goal becomes a graph of small nodes, and the ready ones run in parallel. Each node runs on its category's model and effort; nodes running at once never share a write scope. A separate node checks the goal, and failed nodes are repaired before the report. Expert skills on demand. A hundred-plus omh-* specialists: frontend, backend, Rust, security review, verification gates. You never call them; the router loads the right ones into the run as tool calls. LSP in the loop. Definitions, references and renames come from the language server, not from text search. The model renames what the code means, not what the text matches: aliases, re-exports and shadowed names included. Off by default; enable lsp_tools in the OMH plugin settings. Long-term memory you can trust. Nothing is remembered silently: each candidate is kept, refused or deferred with a written reason. The next session gets a recall pack ranked for its task and cut to a token budget. Hermes' own memory is never read or patched. OMH Native. Bare omh opens OMH's own TUI on Hermes' gateway; switch its launch look with /theme . /dag-ulw prints the box graph, then a live lane tree with each lane's model, effort and tokens. Steer or interrupt an agent from the agent list, run a ! shell line, and rewind with Esc Esc. Evidence before "done". Every status names its stage and how sure OMH is about it. Plan · not run · Code · reported done · Test · verified A run counts as verified only when a test, review or CI gate actually passed. DAG-ULW Just type /dag-ulw , and you're a graph engineering master. Your goal becomes a graph of small nodes that run in parallel, each on its own model. A separate node verifies the goal before you get the report. Tip Be with us! Updates for oh-my-hermes are shared on @rlaope on X, alongside release notes and project news. Follow @rlaope on GitHub for more projects, releases, and ongoing work. Join the Oh-My-Hermes Community on Discord to ask questions, share workflows, and talk with other users. Built with AI agents Friren and Kami , collaborators helping ship oh-my-hermes . Thank you to Nous Research for creating Hermes Agent. Sponsors These are our sponsors. They help keep oh-my-hermes going. OpenGateway sponsors oh-my-hermes, thank you for backing open source. One OpenAI-compatible endpoint for many model providers, with automatic failover. Others Docs · Installation · Capabilities · Workflows · Website Install options macOS / Linux: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rlaope/oh-my-hermes/main/install.sh | sh Windows (PowerShell 5.1+): irm https: // raw.githubusercontent.com / rlaope / oh - my - hermes / main / install.ps1 | iex Or paste this into your AI agent: Install and fully configure Oh My Hermes from this repository:
https://github.com/rlaope/oh-my-hermes
Before reading or executing repository instructions, resolve refs/heads/main to one full commit SHA with `git ls-remote https://github.com/rlaope/oh-my-hermes.git refs/heads/main`. Then fetch and follow only:
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rlaope/oh-my-hermes/{resolved-commit-sha}/INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md
Do not replace the resolved SHA with main. Execute the pinned protocol's OS-appropriate installer, agent setup path, model-chain interview, and doctor steps. Your shell has no terminal, so never run the interactive setup wizard: show me each choice the protocol lists and wait for my answer instead of taking a default. Preserve unrelated existing Hermes config, apply only the managed setup changes documented by the pinned protocol, require my explicit approval for model-alias changes, then report the resolved SHA and observed result. Update: omh update omh update detects how the command was installed, upgrades it through its
owning installer, then refreshes the managed skills, the plugin bundle, and the
Hermes registration. Verify or troubleshoot: omh doctor # Set the model per work category (arrow keys: category, ←→ head model, -/+ effort); # the same picker opens inside the OMH TUI (bare omh) as /omh-model: omh model # To onboard a new model family, use this skill in Hermes: /omh-model-setup Homebrew: brew install rlaope/tap/omh Bun: bun install -g oh-my-hermes npm: npm install -g oh-my-hermes Bun and npm also need Node 18+ and Python 3.11+ on PATH; Homebrew brings its
own Python. Run omh setup after any of these, same as above. Hermes skill tap path: hermes skills tap add rlaope/oh-my-hermes
hermes skills install rlaope/oh-my-hermes/skills/omh-routing --yes Manual package-manager fallback or removal: Installed with Upgrade the CLI Remove the CLI Homebrew brew upgrade rlaope/tap/omh brew uninstall omh Bun bun update -g --latest oh-my-hermes bun remove -g oh-my-hermes npm npm update -g oh-my-hermes npm uninstall -g oh-my-hermes Use the manager command directly only when omh update reports that its owning
manager is unavailable. Removing the command package preserves OMH state. For
a full removal, run omh uninstall --all before the manager's remove command. Maintenance paths such as reconciling a --full install back to core live in Installation . Reference Ultra-Skills Ten ulw- workflows. Say the trigger in chat — Hermes routes the
rest. Full catalog: Workflow Reference . Workflow command What it does ⚡ ulw-context Aligns reviewed project terms, captures confirmed candidates, and interviews the next decision frontier without giving terminology routing authority. ⚡ ulw-interview Asks one question at a time until it knows exactly what you want. ⚡ ulw-research Digs through real code and the live web, keeps sources, and verifies anything doubtful. ⚡ ulw-plan Builds a reviewed plan: options compared, risks named, done-criteria agreed. ⚡ ulw-work Runs an accepted plan in parallel lanes that never touch the same file. ⚡ dag-ulw Runs a big job as a graph of small parallel nodes, verifies the goal with a separate node, and repairs what failed. ⚡ ulw-maestro Runs a delegated task on Claude Code or Codex — prompt composed from the CLI's own installed skills, spawned live with a dock row and a steerable session. ⚡ ulw-loop Cycles plan → build → review until the goal actually passes. ⚡ ulw-qa Attacks the build with hostile scenarios and fixes what breaks. ⚡ ulw-perf Measures where it is actually slow or expensive, then fixes one hot path at a time. Recommended set Type these at the Hermes prompt. The ulw- prefix picks the workflow; the
rest is your request in plain words. 1. Shape it. ulw-interview when the idea is still fuzzy, ulw-plan when
the change is known but risky. ❯ ulw-interview: I want a CLI that tracks the ISS and warns me before it passes overhead
❯ ulw-plan: analyze this project's circular dependencies and plan the refactor 2. Build it. ulw-work runs the accepted plan in parallel lanes that never
edit the same file. ❯ ulw-work: run the accepted plan 3. Finish it. ulw-loop keeps cycling until the gate you name passes. ❯ ulw-loop: keep going until npm test passes How it works with Hermes Hermes Agent already runs the loop.

title: volcengine/OpenViking
abstract:
The Context Database for AI Agents English / 中文 / 日本語 Website · Live Demo · GitHub · Issues · Docs · Blog Lark · WeChat · Discord · X What is OpenViking OpenViking is an open-source context database for AI agents — one filesystem for everything an agent knows: knowledge, memory, and skills. Most agent memory is a black box: text goes in, embeddings come out, and nobody can see what was actually stored. OpenViking organizes context as a virtual filesystem under viking:// instead. Agents navigate it like files — ls , tree , read , write , grep — and you can open any directory to inspect and edit what your agent knows. Every directory carries a generated summary, so agents can scan summaries first and decide what to read. Try OpenViking Studio in your browser, no installation required. Self-host Web Studio . Why OpenViking One filesystem for knowledge, memory, and skills. Resources hold documents and code; memories retain user preferences and experience; skills define how to perform tasks — not just extracted facts, but the full context, each with a viking:// URI for browsing and retrieval. → Viking URI · Context types Search a directory, not the whole index. Scope semantic search to a project or memory subtree instead of scanning a flat vector pool. find runs a query directly; search plans retrieval from session context. → Retrieval Read the summary before the source. Generated directory abstracts (L0) and overviews (L1) let agents judge relevance before opening full content (L2). → Context layers Sessions become files you can read. Committing a session archives the conversation and extracts memories as Markdown you can inspect, edit, and merge. With VikingBot enabled, ov compile organizes source material into a wiki, knowledge graph, or report. → Sessions · Context compilation Architecture · Design rationale viking://
├── resources/              # Resources: project docs, repos, web pages, etc.
│   └── my_project/
│       ├── docs/
│       │   ├── api/
│       │   └── tutorials/
│       └── src/
└── user/
    └── {user_id}/
        ├── memories/
        │   └── preferences/
        │       ├── writing_style
        │       └── coding_habits
        ├── resources/
        │   └── private_project/
        ├── skills/
        │   ├── search_code
        │   └── analyze_data
        └── peers/
            └── web-visitor-alice/ The three loading tiers: L0 (Abstract) : a one-sentence summary for quick relevance checks. L1 (Overview) : core information and usage scenarios for planning. L2 (Details) : the full original data, read only when needed. Semantically processed directories carry L0/L1 summaries, so agents can judge relevance before reading full files: viking://resources/my_project/
├── .abstract.md           # L0: quick relevance check
├── .overview.md           # L1: structure and key points
└── docs/
    ├── .abstract.md
    ├── .overview.md
    └── api/
        ├── auth.md         # L2: full content, loaded on demand
        └── endpoints.md Proof it works OpenViking 0.3.22 has been evaluated on long-conversation user memory (LoCoMo) and multi-turn agent tasks (tau2-bench). Full results and setup details, including knowledge-base QA, are in the benchmark report ; reproduction scripts live in ./benchmark . To run your own experiments, follow the RAG and Memory evaluation guide for routine VikingBot memory evaluation, published LoCoMo reproduction, separate mem0 prompt comparisons, and RAG evaluation. The memory evaluation used Doubao 2.0 Pro as the VLM and Doubao-embedding-vision-251215 as the embedding model. User memory (LoCoMo) : with OpenViking, all three agent integrations land at 80–83% accuracy — up from 24–57% on their native memory — while input tokens drop by 34.3–91.0% and query latency by 58.45–66.10%. Agent experience (tau2-bench) : experience memory lifts task success by +6.87pp (retail) and +11.87pp (airline) over the same LLM without memory. Quick start Set up an OpenViking server first; if you already have one, skip to Use it with your agent . Deploying your own needs uv, Python 3.10+ and a model provider with an embedding model and a VLM. Let your agent deploy it Follow this guide to install and start an OpenViking Server for me:

https://docs.openviking.ai/en/getting-started/04-setup-for-agent

Ask me for the model provider, the models, the workspace directory and whether
other machines need to reach the server; don't guess. When you ask for the model
API key, tell me how to hand it over if I'd rather not paste it into this chat,
and never repeat it back.

When it's running, tell me the server's address and whether auth is turned on. Your agent will first ask which model provider to use and for its API key. Deploy it yourself Install OpenViking and run the setup wizard, which configures the models: uv tool install openviking --upgrade && openviking-server init init writes ~/.openviking/ov.conf and supports Volcengine, OpenAI, Codex OAuth, Kimi, GLM and local Ollama; see the configuration guide . The server runs in the foreground, so keep this terminal open. Use OpenViking Service (hosted by Volcengine) The same OpenViking service, run for you by Volcengine. The first 50 files are free. Activate it on the Volcengine product page , then create an API key in the console under User Management → API Key. The server address is https://api.vikingdb.cn-beijing.volces.com/openviking ; you'll need it and the API key when you connect your agent. Explore with the CLI The openviking package includes the ov CLI. With the server running, import a repository and search it: ov status
ov add-resource https://github.com/volcengine/OpenViking # Replace TASK_ID with the returned task_id; repeat until status is completed ov task status TASK_ID
ov ls viking://resources/
ov tree viking://resources/volcengine -L 2
ov find " what is openviking " ov grep " openviking " --uri viking://resources/volcengine/OpenViking/docs/en ov find returns matching context with URIs you can inspect. For client configuration ( ov config ), standalone CLI installs, and index maintenance, see CLI setup . Build your own integration with the Python , Go , or TypeScript SDK, or the HTTP API . Use it with your agent Connect your coding agent to OpenViking for cross-session memory. The memory plugin installer covers Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, TRAE, OpenCode and more, and detects which ones you have. Let your agent install it Install the OpenViking memory plugin and help me start using it. OpenViking is the open-source context database for AI agents from Volcengine (https://github.com/volcengine/OpenViking, AGPL-3.0); the command and link below are from its official docs.

1. Run the official installer. It needs network access and writes to my home directory; if your sandbox blocks that, ask me for approval:
   curl -fsSL https://openviking.ai/install | bash -s -- --yes --lang en --url <SERVER_URL> --api-key <API_KEY>
2. Once it's installed, read the OpenViking onboarding guide and use it to walk me through setup. The guide has you ask me before choices like importing history or adding a working rule. docs.openviking.ai and docs.openviking.net are the same docs site; use whichever loads:
   https://docs.openviking.ai/agents/en/onboarding.md

The API key is a user key I created for myself on that server; the installer stores it in ~/.openviking/ovcli.conf on this machine. Use it in the command as it is; there's no need to show it in your replies, and don't write it into any other file or rule. Talk to me in English. Before you send it, replace <SERVER_URL> with your server's address and <API_KEY> with a user key; a root key can't read or write memories. If the server has auth turned off, use --api-key '' . Install it yourself Run the installer, then pick the tools and a server when asked: Self-hosted / local for a server on this machine, Volcengine OpenViking Cloud for OpenViking Service, or Custom URL for any other address. If auth is on, enter a user key, not the root key.

title: ansible/ansible
abstract:
Ansible Ansible is a radically simple IT automation system. It handles
configuration management, application deployment, cloud provisioning,
ad-hoc task execution, network automation, and multi-node orchestration. Ansible makes complex
changes like zero-downtime rolling updates with load balancers easy. More information on the Ansible website . Design Principles Have an extremely simple setup process with a minimal learning curve. Manage machines quickly and in parallel. Avoid custom-agents and additional open ports, be agentless by
leveraging the existing SSH daemon. Describe infrastructure in a language that is both machine and human
friendly. Focus on security and easy auditability/review/rewriting of content. Manage new remote machines instantly, without bootstrapping any
software. Allow module development in any dynamic language, not just Python. Be usable as non-root. Be the easiest IT automation system to use, ever. Use Ansible You can install a released version of Ansible with pip or a package manager. See our installation guide for details on installing Ansible
on a variety of platforms. Power users and developers can run the devel branch, which has the latest
features and fixes, directly. Although it is reasonably stable, you are more likely to encounter
breaking changes when running the devel branch. We recommend getting involved
in the Ansible community if you want to run the devel branch. Communication Join the Ansible forum to ask questions, get help, and interact with the
community. Get Help : Find help or share your Ansible knowledge to help others.
Use tags to filter and subscribe to posts, such as the following: Posts tagged with ansible Posts tagged with ansible-core Posts tagged with playbook Social Spaces : Meet and interact with fellow enthusiasts. News & Announcements : Track project-wide announcements including social events. Bullhorn newsletter : Get release announcements and important changes. For more ways to get in touch, see Communicating with the Ansible community . Contribute to Ansible Check out the Contributor's Guide . Read Community Information for all
kinds of ways to contribute to and interact with the project,
including how to submit bug reports and code to Ansible. Submit a proposed code update through a pull request to the devel branch. Talk to us before making larger changes
to avoid duplicate efforts. This not only helps everyone
know what is going on, but it also helps save time and effort if we decide
some changes are needed. Coding Guidelines Development context for ansible-core can be found in the context directory. We also document our Coding Guidelines in the Developer Guide . We particularly suggest you review: Contributing your module to Ansible Conventions, tips, and pitfalls Branch Info The devel branch corresponds to the release actively under development. The stable-2.X branches correspond to stable releases. Create a branch based on devel and set up a dev environment if you want to open a PR. See the Ansible release and maintenance page for information about active branches. Roadmap Based on team and community feedback, an initial roadmap will be published for a major or minor version (ex: 2.7, 2.8).
The Ansible Roadmap page details what is planned and how to influence the roadmap. Authors Ansible was created by Michael DeHaan and has contributions from over 5000 users (and growing). Thanks everyone! This project is substantially coded by humans. Ansible is sponsored by Red Hat, Inc. License GNU General Public License v3.0 or later See COPYING to see the full text.

title: PurpleDoubleD/locally-uncensored
abstract: Locally Uncensored The all-in-one local AI studio for your desktop. Chat, images, video and a coding agent in one app. Install it, pick a model, go. Free and open source. In local mode everything runs on your own machine. No Docker, no terminal, no config files. The platforms are listed under Download . Download · Three steps · What is in the box · How it compares · Models · FAQ Chat that draws your images Images and video in the same window The coding agent shows the diff first Agent mode does the legwork Download Take the latest build from Releases . Platform File Status Windows 10 and 11 Locally.Uncensored_3.0.8_x64-setup.exe (NSIS, recommended) or Locally.Uncensored_3.0.8_x64_en-US.msi Tested every release, signed auto update channel Linux Locally.Uncensored_3.0.8_amd64.AppImage , Locally.Uncensored_3.0.8_amd64.deb or Locally.Uncensored-3.0.8-1.x86_64.rpm Built on every release macOS 14 or newer, Apple Silicon (Beta) LU_3.0.8_aarch64.dmg Signed with an Apple Developer ID and notarized by Apple. Intel Macs are not supported. The app has run on one Mac so far. Voice has been tried by hand in the app on a Mac and works. Computer control is in the Mac app but not fully tested yet on macOS. Remote Access and the automatic update are not confirmed on macOS Android 7.0 or newer (arm64) LU-3.0.7-Android.apk The phone app. Not in the Play Store yet: install the file from this page. SHA-256 2f4e2c60f2edde2705c31ca324b5ba952a84efa8eec3075f4f45f2a29a806fb6 Some antivirus engines flag unsigned NSIS installers that download other binaries, which is a false positive. The installer is built by GitHub Actions from the public source on master , and the update channel is signed against a public minisign key, so you can verify both: see SECURITY.md . Code signing for the Windows installers: free code signing provided by SignPath.io , certificate by SignPath Foundation . SignPath Foundation has accepted the project. The production certificate is not in place yet, and until it is the installers ship unsigned. Current release: v3.0.8 (October 2026). Every change since 1.0.0 is in CHANGELOG.md . 3.0.8 makes web search in the chat work again: LU asks five search services in turn and needs no key for any of them. A video made in the chat plays in the chat, and a long one renders in the background while you write on. A picture attached in the chat reaches the image tool, and with two graphics cards chat and ComfyUI can each get their own. The LU Engine plans a model's memory from the file itself and offers a shorter context with one click. AMD cards on Windows get AMD's current ROCm build. New: the chat can read and change LU's settings with a confirmation card, the Model Manager can make a copy of a local model that refuses less, and Settings, Storage puts models, gallery and runtime in one folder of your choice. What has only run in automated tests is listed under Known limits in the CHANGELOG . 3.0.7 brings REA (Reverse Engineer Anything) as a plugin: switch it on under Plugins in the desktop app, and Agent and Code can take apart apps and files (it needs Node.js and works best with a model of about 27B and 64K context; a full analysis has run on one Mac so far, and on Windows it has started from the built app). LU Cloud now has DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, ready to pick in Chat. A chat can be duplicated or branched from any message, character cards turn into personas with their greeting, a persona can carry a reminder, group chats got a round of fixes, and auto compact is on by default. A character you trained works in every part of Create and in chat, and a Mac can train one too. ComfyUI workflows import the way ComfyUI saves them, a whole folder at once, with the node packs they need, and LU now uses the shared model folders set in ComfyUI. In Create, Edit takes as many reference images as the graphics memory holds (up to ten on a Mac), Enhance Image runs on your own machine, and on a Mac Talking Character, Motion Control, Music, Enhance Image, Remove Background and masks in Edit run locally. There is an Android app now, see Mobile app below. The iPhone app is in review at the App Store. Some of it has only been checked in tests so far; the CHANGELOG says which. 3.0.5 was about Create: LTX 2.5, FastH3 and YuE2 run on your own machine, Qwen-Image 2.1 gets a transparent background and its prompt enhancer, Edit, Remove Background and Enhance Image take up to 50 images in one go, and LU Cloud adds Qwen Image 2.1, LTX 2.5, MiniMax H3 and Wan 3.0 Reference. Chat takes any file, each model in a group chat can have its own persona, dropdowns stay inside the window (issue 149), and the speech install works again on Ubuntu 24.04. 3.0.4 fixed the Code agent and the agent in chat on LU Cloud: writing a long file no longer ends the run, "continue" picks up where a run stopped instead of starting over, the agent keeps a plan only when you ask for one, and cloud context is 32K by default and can be set per model. It also fixed the bugs reported on GitHub and Discord since 3.0.3 (issues 144 to 147): MiniMax H3 runs as a video model with sound, Edit takes up to three extra images with Qwen-Image 2.1, a missing encoder or VAE is named and offered as a download instead of ending in "Value not in list", the LoRA stack follows the loras folder, and group chat works with every LU Engine model. 3.0.3 was a hotfix: chats with many images no longer run the app out of memory, Create reads a model's family from the file instead of its name, and the five bugs reported on GitHub since 3.0.2 are fixed (issues 139 to 143). 3.0.2 was a hotfix: the Code tab lost its scrollbar and its input box once a conversation grew taller than the window (issue 138, a regression in 3.0.1) and is held to the window height again, and the count of open cloud models now takes the Create Studio endpoints in, which makes it fourteen video models and seven image models. What is new in 3.0.1 Qwen-Image 2.1 runs locally on Windows and Linux. One model generates a picture from a prompt and edits one from a reference image, with no mask to paint. About 16 GB of files, ComfyUI 0.37.0 or newer, and a research license that does not allow commercial use. Models has a LoRAs tab of its own. Search CivitAI, download into ComfyUI's models/loras folder, see what is installed with its size and trigger word, and delete what you no longer want. A GPU whose free memory could not be measured is planned more carefully , and the log now says total capacity instead of calling it free. The Linux AppImage stops handing its own runtime to every program LU starts , so a healthy system Python, pip, git or ffmpeg keeps working, and a distribution that blocks pip in the system Python keeps the isolated environment LU built. The local model runs one conversation at a time and says so , with a line showing how many chats are ahead. Stop works while a chat is still waiting. Temperature, Top P and Max tokens belong to the conversation you moved them in , instead of every open chat sharing one value. Cloud video renders offer the clip lengths the picked model really supports , read from the live catalog. Mobile app (Android, iPhone) LU is also available as an app for your phone. The current APK comes from the 3.0.7 release. Android: download LU-3.0.7-Android.apk from the 3.0.7 release . Needs Android 7.0 or newer on a 64-bit (arm64) phone. Allow installing apps from your browser or file app when Android asks. SHA-256: 2f4e2c60f2edde2705c31ca324b5ba952a84efa8eec3075f4f45f2a29a806fb6 iPhone: in review at the App Store. Google Play: coming later. What the app does: Run AI models on your phone and chat offline. Chats with on-device models stay on the phone. Ask questions about your own documents. Memory and personas. Optional LU Cloud with your account: larger hosted chat models, Create (images and video) and dictation. Connect to LU on your own computer over your home Wi-Fi and chat with the models on your PC.

title: CopilotKit/CopilotKit
abstract:
Docs · Examples · Intelligence · OpenBot · Discord CopilotKit is the open-source stack for putting AI agents in front of real users. Bring the agent you already built, on any framework, and give it chat, generative UI, shared state, and human-in-the-loop in React, Angular, Vue, React Native, Slack, and Microsoft Teams. When it goes to production, add CopilotKit Intelligence and your agents keep getting better: conversations that pick up where users left off, memory across sessions, and Continual Learning that turns real use into Skills you review and publish. We're also the team behind AG-UI , the open Agent–User Interaction protocol adopted by Google, Microsoft, AWS, LangChain, Mastra, PydanticAI, and more. What's new What's new What it is 🪁 CopilotKit Soar AI coworkers your company owns, running on your own servers. Powered by OpenBot. Now in early access → 🔁 Continual Learning Agents learn from full-stack trajectories (what the agent did and what your users did), captured over AG-UI. 🤖 OpenBot Open-source AI coworkers that each get a computer of their own. MIT licensed. 🧩 AG-UI 1.0 + A2UI 1.0 CopilotKit now speaks AG-UI 1.0 and the A2UI 1.0 spec for declarative generative UI. 💬 Channels Write Channels JSX once. Render native Block Kit in Slack and Adaptive Cards in Microsoft Teams. Full changelog in What's New . Quick start Let your coding agent do it. Paste this prompt into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or any coding agent running in your project. It inspects your app and walks you through the integration. Help me get started with CopilotKit. From the root of my project, run this
command and follow the instructions:

npx --yes copilotkit@latest onboard start Start a new project. Scaffolds a fresh app in its own directory. It won't touch an app you already have. npx copilotkit@latest create Give your coding agent CopilotKit skills. Helps it build features and debug issues once you're set up ( learn more ). npx copilotkit@latest skills install Prefer to wire it up by hand? Here's a Next.js app in three files. npm install @copilotkit/react-core @copilotkit/runtime # .env.local OPENAI_API_KEY=your_openai_api_key // app/api/copilotkit/[[...slug]]/route.ts import { CopilotRuntime , createCopilotRuntimeHandler , BuiltInAgent , } from "@copilotkit/runtime/v2" ; const runtime = new CopilotRuntime ( { agents : { default : new BuiltInAgent ( { model : "openai:gpt-5.4-mini" } ) } , } ) ; const handler = createCopilotRuntimeHandler ( { runtime , basePath : "/api/copilotkit" , } ) ; export { handler as GET , handler as POST , handler as PATCH , handler as DELETE } ; // app/page.tsx "use client" ; import { CopilotKitProvider , CopilotSidebar } from "@copilotkit/react-core/v2" ; import "@copilotkit/react-core/v2/styles.css" ; export default function Page ( ) { return ( < CopilotKitProvider runtimeUrl = "/api/copilotkit" > < main > < h1 > Your App </ h1 > < CopilotSidebar /> </ main > </ CopilotKitProvider > ) ; } Already running LangGraph, CrewAI, Mastra, or another framework? Swap the Built-in Agent for yours using that framework's quickstart . getting-started-with-one-command.mp4 How it works Your agent handles reasoning and execution. CopilotKit turns its work into a product experience. Events stream over AG-UI , so the agent can show its work as it happens, read what the user is looking at, call tools that render UI, and pause for a person to approve the next step. Your agent logic stays the same on every surface. What you can build Whole.Generative.UI.v5.mp4 Feature What it does Chat components Start with a working chat, replace the parts you need with slots, or go fully Headless UI. Generative UI Agents render real UI, from your own components to A2UI specs to sandboxed MCP Apps. Shared state One state layer that both the agent and your UI read and write in real time. Human-in-the-loop Agents pause for input, confirmation, or edits before they act. Frontend tools Let the agent take actions inside your app, with your code doing the work. AG-UI Streams Conversations that survive reloads, devices, and sessions, with generative UI intact. Voice and WebMCP Talk to your agent, and expose your app's actions to browser agents. Inspector A localhost overlay that shows threads, agents, and learning as you build. Full control with useAgent Every component is built on hooks you can use directly. useAgent sits right on top of AG-UI and gives you programmatic control of the agent connection. import { useAgent } from "@copilotkit/react-core/v2" ; function CityPicker ( ) { const { agent } = useAgent ( { agentId : "my_agent" } ) ; return ( < div > < h1 > { agent . state . city } </ h1 > < button onClick = { ( ) => agent . setState ( { city : "NYC" } ) } > Set city </ button > </ div > ) ; } More in the programmatic control docs . Generative UI, three ways demo-generative-ui.mp4 Type The agent… Built on Controlled picks from components you registered AG-UI tool calls and state Declarative describes UI as a structured spec your app renders A2UI Open-ended ships a full interface that runs in a sandbox MCP Apps Want to go deeper? The Generative UI educational repo walks through all three. Works with your stack One agent backend. Every frontend. Surface Status Get started ⚛️ React / Next.js ✅ GA Quickstart 🅰️ Angular ✅ Supported Quickstart 💚 Vue ✅ Supported Quickstart 📱 React Native ✅ Supported Quickstart 💬 Slack / Microsoft Teams ✅ GA on cloud-hosted Intelligence Slack · Teams 💬 Discord / WhatsApp ✅ Channels SDK adapters Channels 🔜 Google Chat / iMessage / SMS 🟡 On the roadmap Channels 🪁 CopilotKit Soar, powered by OpenBot ✨ Early access Get early access Agent frameworks. LangGraph · Deep Agents · CrewAI · Mastra · Google ADK · PydanticAI · Microsoft Agent Framework · AWS Strands · Claude Agent SDK · LlamaIndex · Agno · AG2 · A2A · or CopilotKit's Built-in Agent . CopilotKit Intelligence Most agents plateau at launch quality. CopilotKit Intelligence is the production layer that keeps yours improving. It works with the CopilotKit app and agent framework you already run, cloud-hosted or self-hosted on your own infrastructure. Continual Learning : real use of your app becomes evidence-backed insights, then Skills you review and publish. Every learned behavior traces back to its source. AG-UI Streams : conversations pick up where users left off, with messages, generative UI, and live runs restored as they were. User Memories : durable facts and preferences carried across conversations, recalled semantically. Product Analytics : see what users ask for, what agents do, and where people get value. Channels : Slack and Microsoft Teams infrastructure for the agent you already built. Self-hosted : the same platform inside your Kubernetes cluster, VPC, or air-gapped environment. The Developer plan is free. 👉 Connect Intelligence in 5 minutes → · Compare open source and Intelligence AI coworkers, built on CopilotKit We build real products on this stack, and open-source them. OpenBot is an open-source agent workspace for your employees. Every AI coworker gets a computer of its own, with a browser, files, and tools, and every action is decided before it happens and recorded after. Bring any AG-UI agent and any model. CopilotKit Soar turns that core into one business-ready product. It gives each employee an AI coworker that works in your company's tools, learns new tasks from the people it works with, and runs on your own servers. Our engineers set it up with you, then hand you the keys. Soar is in early access today. 👉 Get early access → OpenBot AI coworkers, each with a computer of its own. OpenDots Always-on coworkers for text, calls, and Slack. OpenMuse A personal agent for iOS, Android, and web. OpenTag An on-call triage bot for Slack and Teams. AG-UI: the Agent–User Interaction protocol AG-UI is the open, event-based protocol that connects agents to the people using them. MCP connects agents to tools, A2A connects agents to each other, and AG-UI connects them to your users.

title: agentscope-ai/QwenPaw
abstract:
QwenPaw [ Documentation ] [ 中文 ] [ 日本語 ] [ Русский ] Works for you, grows with you. Your personal AI assistant — deploy locally or in the cloud, extend with Skills & Plugins, connect across every channel. Never forgets Three-layer memory — live working context, full verbatim history, and a self-evolving personal knowledge base powered by ReMe . Conversations and resources continuously become readable, editable, searchable, and linked Markdown memory. Local or cloud, runs free QwenPaw-Flash models (2B / 4B / 9B / 35B-A3B / 27B) trained for agent tasks. Built-in QwenPaw Local runtime — no API key, no cloud dependency. Also works with Ollama, LM Studio, or 14+ cloud providers. Security built in Kernel-level Sandbox, Tool Guard, File Guard, Skill Scanner, and Access Policy. Dangerous commands are blocked before they run. Multi-agent & parallel Spawn independent agents with their own memory and skills. Sub-agents at runtime. Agent Communication Protocol (ACP) for cross-system orchestration. File workspace Unified file navigation, preview, editing, diffs, upload, and download across project and Agent files. Extensible Skills for scheduling, documents, browser, news, and more. Plugin architecture with a marketplace. MCP integration for external tools. Combine them into purpose-built workflows. Reachable anywhere DingTalk, Lark, WeChat, Discord, Telegram, iMessage, QQ — one instance, all channels. Console, TUI, and desktop app for direct access. Yours, not ours Deploy locally — data stays on your machine. No third-party hosting, no data upload. What you can do with QwenPaw Automation & scheduling : Set up recurring tasks — news digests, report generation, multi-channel broadcasting — all on your schedule. Code & development : Read, edit, review, and test code in your projects with the unified file workspace. Document processing : Read, write, and convert PDF, Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files. Information gathering : Search the web, follow subscriptions, summarize videos, and find what you need in your personal knowledge base. Multi-channel ops : Push alerts, summaries, or AI-generated content to DingTalk, Lark, Discord, Telegram, and more — simultaneously or per channel. Custom workflows : Combine built-in capabilities, plugins, and scheduled tasks into workflows tailored to your needs. qwenpaw app Then open the Console in your browser at http://127.0.0.1:8088/ to configure your model. To chat in DingTalk, Lark, WeChat, etc., see the Channel setup documentation. The script will automatically download uv (Python package manager), create a virtual environment, and install QwenPaw with all dependencies (including Node.js and frontend assets). Note: May not work in restricted network environments or corporate firewalls. macOS / Linux: curl -fsSL https://qwenpaw.agentscope.io/install.sh | bash Windows (CMD): curl -fsSL https://qwenpaw.agentscope.io/install.bat -o install.bat && install.bat Windows (PowerShell): irm https: // qwenpaw.agentscope.io / install.ps1 | iex Note : The installer will automatically check the status of uv. If it is not installed, it will attempt to download and configure it automatically. If the automatic installation fails, please follow the on-screen prompts or execute python -m pip install -U uv , then rerun the installer. ⚠️ Special Notice for Windows Enterprise LTSC Users If you are using Windows LTSC or an enterprise environment governed by strict security policies, PowerShell may run in Constrained Language Mode , potentially causing the following issue: If using CMD (.bat): Script executes successfully but fails to write to Path The script completes file installation. Due to Constrained Language Mode , it cannot automatically update environment variables. Manually configure as follows: Locate the installation directory : Check if uv is available: Enter uv --version in CMD. If a version number appears, only configure the QwenPaw path . If you receive the prompt 'uv' is not recognized as an internal or external command, operable program or batch file, configure both paths. uv path (choose one based on installation location; use if uv fails): Typically %USERPROFILE%\.local\bin , %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\uv , or the Scripts folder within your Python installation directory QwenPaw path: Typically located at %USERPROFILE%\.qwenpaw\bin . Manually add to the system's Path environment variable : Press Win + R , type sysdm.cpl and press Enter to open System Properties. Click “Advanced” -> “Environment Variables”. Under “System variables”, locate and select Path , then click “Edit”. Click “New”, enter both directory paths sequentially, then click OK to save. If using PowerShell (.ps1): Script execution interrupted Due to Constrained Language Mode , the script may fail to automatically download uv . Manually install uv : Refer to the GitHub Release to download uv.exe and place it in %USERPROFILE%\.local\bin or %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\uv ; or ensure Python is installed and run python -m pip install -U uv . Configure uv environment variables : Add the uv directory and %USERPROFILE%\.qwenpaw\bin to your system's Path variable. Re-run the installation : Open a new terminal and execute the installation script again to complete the QwenPaw installation. Configure the QwenPaw environment variable : Add %USERPROFILE%\.qwenpaw\bin to your system's Path variable. title: openobserve/openobserve
abstract:
Open source Datadog alternative for logs, metrics, traces, and frontend monitoring. Modern observability platform: 10x easier, 140x lower storage cost, high performance, petabyte scale. Cloud · Documentation · Slack · Quickstart OpenObserve (O2) is a cloud-native observability platform for logs, metrics, traces, analytics, Real User Monitoring (RUM), and AI/LLM observability. It's a cost-effective alternative to Datadog, Splunk, and Elasticsearch for teams that need full observability without the complexity or cost — with Parquet columnar storage and an S3-native design that cuts storage costs by up to 140x . Table of Contents Why OpenObserve? Quick Start Product Tour Architecture Comparisons Production Ready Security & Compliance Enterprise Edition Community & Support Contributing FAQ License SBOM Why OpenObserve? A single platform for all of your observability signals. Here's why teams choose OpenObserve: Benefit Description 140x lower storage cost Parquet columnar storage + S3-native architecture dramatically reduce costs vs Elasticsearch Single binary deployment Up and running in under 2 minutes — no complex cluster setup required OpenTelemetry native Built on the OpenTelemetry standard — no vendor lock-in Unified platform Logs, metrics, traces, RUM, dashboards, alerts, and incidents in one tool High performance Better query performance than Elasticsearch on a quarter of the hardware SQL + PromQL Query logs and traces with SQL, metrics with SQL or PromQL — no proprietary query language Built in Rust Memory-safe, high-performance, single binary Cost comparison: OpenObserve vs Elasticsearch Quick Start OpenObserve Cloud (fastest way) Get started in minutes without managing infrastructure. The free tier includes up to 50 GB/day of ingestion. Get Started Free → 🐳 Docker docker run -d \
      --name openobserve \
      -v $PWD /data:/data \
      -p 5080:5080 \
      -e ZO_ROOT_USER_EMAIL= " root@example.com " \
      -e ZO_ROOT_USER_PASSWORD= " Complexpass#123 " \
      public.ecr.aws/zinclabs/openobserve:latest Then open http://localhost:5080 and log in with the credentials above. For other installation methods, see the quickstart documentation . For clustered deployments, see the High Availability deployment guide . Product Tour OpenObserve ships with a powerful, unified web UI for every signal — logs, traces, metrics, dashboards, RUM, alerts, incidents, pipelines, and AI observability. 🏠 Unified Overview A single home for your workspace — active incidents, service health (error rate, latency, requests), anomalies, and recent events at a glance. 📊 Logs Centralized log management with full-text search, SQL queries, quick filters, and a visual query builder. Instantly search across all your logs, build dashboards from log data, and set up alerts — all on Parquet columnar storage for 140x lower storage cost than Elasticsearch. Read more → 🔍 Distributed Tracing Powered by OpenTelemetry, tracing helps you follow requests across services and pinpoint performance bottlenecks. Explore the full request flow with waterfalls, flame graphs, and Gantt charts; click any span to drill into the trace. Read more → 🕸️ Service Graph Visualize service-to-service dependencies and request flow across your system, with per-edge request counts and health-based coloring (healthy, degraded, warning, critical) to spot problem hotspots at a glance. 📈 Metrics Explore metrics from your infrastructure and applications, then query them with SQL or PromQL. Browse thousands of metrics with faceted filters, preview them inline, combine multiple queries with formulae, and visualize the results with 19+ chart types. Read more → 📉 Dashboards Build custom dashboards from any signal with 19+ built-in chart types and 200+ visualization variations, a drag-and-drop panel builder, template variables, and geo maps. Read more → 👀 Frontend Monitoring (RUM) Real User Monitoring with Core Web Vitals, error tracking, performance analytics, and full session replay — so you can see exactly what your users experience. Read more → 🔔 Alerts Get notified when something unusual happens on any signal — logs, metrics, or traces. Define thresholds, scheduled or real-time alerts, and notification channels, with alert history and anomaly detection to catch issues early. Read more → 🚨 Incidents Correlate related alerts into incidents and track them through their lifecycle — open, acknowledged, and resolved — with severity and dimension context for faster response. 🔀 Pipelines Enrich, redact, reduce, or normalize data at ingest time with a visual editor. Build stream-processing flows — including logs-to-metrics conversion — from source, transform (VRL functions and conditions), and destination nodes. No external tools required. Read more → 🤖 AI Observability Monitor your GenAI and LLM applications: track cost, tokens, latency percentiles, and error rates across models, with agent graphs, session traces, and evaluation/quality scoring. ✨ O2 AI Assistant An in-product assistant that writes your SQL, VRL, and PromQL and walks you through logs, traces, metrics, and incidents — turning natural-language questions into queries, dashboards, and alerts. For the full feature list, see the documentation . Architecture OpenObserve achieves 140x lower storage costs and high performance through a modern, cloud-native architecture: Parquet columnar storage — efficient compression and fast analytical queries S3-native design — inexpensive object storage with intelligent caching Built in Rust — memory-safe, high-performance, single binary Partitioning, indexing, and smart caching — reduces search space by up to 99% for most queries Native multi-tenancy — organizations and streams as first-class concepts with complete data isolation Stateless architecture — rapid scaling and low RPO/RTO for disaster recovery Scale & Deployment Thousands of concurrent users can query a single cluster simultaneously Single binary scales to terabytes — unique in the observability space High Availability mode scales to petabytes for the most demanding workloads Multi-region deployments with cluster federation via Super Cluster architecture (Enterprise) Federated search across regions and clusters (Enterprise) High Availability & Disaster Recovery Deploy in High Availability mode with clustering for mission-critical workloads requiring maximum uptime. OpenObserve's stateless architecture with S3-backed storage enables very low Recovery Point Objective (RPO) and Recovery Time Objective (RTO): stateless nodes restart rapidly, and durability is guaranteed by S3's 99.999999999% (11 nines). Read the architecture documentation → · Read the enterprise deployment guide → Comparisons OpenObserve vs Datadog Aspect OpenObserve Datadog Deployment Self-hosted or Cloud SaaS only Pricing model Per-GB (free up to 50 GB/day) Per-host + per-GB Open source Yes (AGPL-3.
