title: Grace Blackwell needs a new scheduler: 27% more usable GPUs from the same racks
abstract:
Not all high-speed interconnects are created equal, and using the wrong one can be quite costly: running the same distributed training job over InfiniBand rather than NVLink can degrade performance by 43% . Historically, NVLink was limited to communication within a single node, meaning that multi-node AI workloads were forced to communicate over InfiniBand or a cloud equivalent (EFA on AWS, GPUDirect-TCPX on GCP). NVIDIA’s NVL72 systems remove this limitation by connecting all 72 GPUs in a rack with a unified NVLink fabric, so GPUs on different nodes can exchange data with an order of magnitude more bandwidth. However, maximizing the benefits of NVL72 systems is highly dependent on workload placement: a multi-node job spread across racks is still bottlenecked by InfiniBand. Preserving rack-locality gets harder as hardware failures take nodes offline and jobs finishing at different times scatter free capacity across racks. This blog covers the communication bottleneck in large-scale training and inference, the NVL72 rack-scale fabric, and slice sizing for resilience to GPU failures, as well as how the SkyPilot Platform keeps multi-node jobs rack-local through topology-aware placement, in-place recovery from hardware failures, and automatic defragmentation of shared clusters. Training at scale is a communication problem # Frontier training jobs run across thousands of GPUs. Doing so requires answering two questions: How do you shard your model across GPUs to ensure that it can actually run? Given your compute budget, how many copies of the sharded model can you run to maximize training throughput? The first question is typically answered with a combination of: Tensor Parallelism (TP): splitting a layer’s weight matrices across GPUs Expert Parallelism (EP): placing a mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer’s experts on different GPUs Pipeline Parallelism (PP): splitting a model layer-wise across GPUs The answer to the second question sets the degree of Data Parallelism (DP): the number of copies of the sharded model that train in parallel, each on a different slice of the training data. Of these parallelism strategies, tensor parallelism’s all-reduce and expert parallelism’s all-to-all communication patterns sit on the critical path during training, making them the most important to keep on NVLink (§9.1.2). Tensor Parallelism Tensor parallelism splits the weight matrices inside each layer across GPUs, so every GPU only stores and computes a slice of each layer. Transformer layers are made up of two blocks: self-attention and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP). At its core, each block is two matrix multiplications (GEMMs) in a row. Megatron-LM (§3) showed that by partitioning a block’s first GEMM column-wise and its second GEMM row-wise, the GPUs only need to synchronize via all-reduce once per block, after the second GEMM, instead of after each one. Figure 1. Tensor parallelism across two GPUs. A is split column-wise, so each GPU computes its own slice of y without communicating. B is split row-wise to match, so each GPU produces a partial z, and one all-reduce sums the partial results. Even with this optimization, tensor parallelism still requires two all-reduces per transformer layer during the forward pass. These all-reduce steps sit on the critical path during training because they cannot be fully overlapped with computation. As a result, tensor parallelism is typically kept on NVLink: Hugging Face measured a 43% drop in training throughput when it moved off NVLink onto InfiniBand. Expert Parallelism In a mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer, the MLP block is replaced by many smaller MLPs, called experts, and a router that sends each token to a small subset of experts. Expert parallelism splits MoE layers such that these small, independent experts are placed on different GPUs. Under expert parallelism, each MoE layer requires two all-to-all communication steps during the forward pass, dispatch and combine. A router selects the top- k experts for each token and dispatches tokens to the GPUs that have those experts in memory. Each GPU then computes its local experts on the tokens it received via a single grouped matrix multiplication. Finally, the expert outputs are sent back to each token's original GPU and combined. Figure 2. Expert parallelism distributes experts across GPUs. The all-to-all communication dispatches tokens to their assigned experts and combines results. (Source: NVIDIA , Figure 4.) As models add more MoE layers and route each token to more experts, the volume of all-to-all traffic grows, introducing a communication bottleneck. Training an MoE model with 64-way expert parallelism spreads each MoE layer’s experts across 64 GPUs. On standard 8-GPU servers, that moves the all-to-all traffic off high-bandwidth NVLink and through much narrower InfiniBand interconnects where unoptimized communication can consume up to 60% of training time (§1.2). On NVL72 systems, all 64 GPUs stay within a single NVLink domain, effectively eliminating the communication bottleneck (§9.2.2). Inference needs fast inter-node networking too # The parallelism techniques discussed above are not unique to training. Beyond enabling inference engines to serve models that are too large for a single GPU, model parallelism can also improve throughput. Splitting a model's weights across more GPUs frees up memory for the KV cache, so the engine can process more concurrent requests or support larger context windows . In some cases, the freed memory grows faster than the number of GPUs: in one vLLM benchmark, splitting a model tensor-parallel across two GPUs increased the amount of KV cache blocks by 13.9x and delivered 3.9x more throughput. Figure 3. GPU memory breakdown for Llama-3.1-70B on one vs. two H100s. (Data: vLLM .) Expert parallelism follows the same logic. With a low degree of expert parallelism, each GPU holds many experts, leaving less room for the KV cache. WideEP, which refers to expert-parallel configurations spanning multiple nodes, significantly reduces the number of experts per GPU. The trade-off is network traffic: every all-to-all now spans more GPUs. On standard 8-GPU servers, an expert-parallel group can span at most eight GPUs before it has to communicate over InfiniBand, where per-GPU bandwidth drops 18x . NVL72 removes this limit by keeping all 72 GPUs in a rack on NVLink. When serving DeepSeek-R1 at interactive speeds, GB200 NVL72 with 32-way expert parallelism delivers up to 4.4x higher throughput per GPU than 8-GPU B200 servers, which are capped at 8-way. The rack is the new server # NVL72 extends NVLink from a single node to the entire rack, so the whole rack acts like a gigantic accelerator with shared memory . Figure 4. The NVLink hierarchy within an NVL72 rack. (Source: NVIDIA , Figure 1.) Every GPU on the NVL72 rack has 18 NVLink ports each delivering 100 GB/s of bidirectional bandwidth, which sums up to a total of 1.8 TB/s for each GPU . Each NVLink port on a given GPU maps to one of 18 NVSwitch chips that power the rack's fabric backplane. Because each NVSwitch chip accepts 72 NVLink lines, one from each of the GPUs, the aggregate internal bandwidth within the rack is 130 TB/s. Figure 5. Each GPU connects one NVLink port to each of the rack's 18 NVSwitch chips. (Source: NADDOD .) This network topology ensures that the fabric is fully non-blocking, meaning that any GPU in the rack can transmit data to any other GPU with uniform latency, making it ideal for large-scale distributed AI workloads. Figure 6. The NVSwitch fabric is fully non-blocking. Any GPU can communicate with any other GPU in the rack at full bandwidth with the same latency. (Source: NVIDIA , Figure 1) Sometimes less is more: using less nodes in each rack significantly improves reliability # With NVL72 systems, it is tempting to allocate entire 18-node racks to workloads to maximize cluster utilization.

(106 points, 18 comments on Hacker News)

title: Claude Code regularly sends each background agent’s transcript to its model
abstract:
Claude Code burns ~15–20% of your tokens on a 3-word status line. Here's how to turn it off by Flamerix AI · MIT License Tested on Linux, Claude Code 2.1.257–2.1.312; macOS reported working by others (see Tested versions). The binary is not modified ( BUN_OPTIONS=--preload ). An update can silently undo it, so see Verify. TL;DR Every ~30 seconds, Claude Code re-sends each background agent's full transcript to the model just
to fill that agent's status line in the agents panel. no-agent-summary.js is a Bun --preload that stops that timer without modifying the Claude Code binary. curl -fsSL https://gist.githubusercontent.com/flamerix-ai/c3905705cc4205e5de3011fa2e74efce/raw/no-agent-summary.js -o ~ /.local/share/no-agent-summary.js
claude daemon stop --any
BUN_OPTIONS= " ${BUN_OPTIONS : + $BUN_OPTIONS } --preload= $HOME /.local/share/no-agent-summary.js " claude To make it permanent for every Claude Code process, see Install . Contents The problem The fix (how it works) Which processes it touches Install Env Nuances Verify (after every update) Fail-open Effect Tested versions Why there is no setting for this Timeline (2026) Changelog License and disclaimer The problem Every ~30 seconds, for every background agent, Claude Code sends that agent's entire
transcript to the agent's own model (usually Opus) and asks it to "describe your most recent
action in 3-5 words". The answer only updates the agent's status line in the agents panel; it
never reaches the model or your conversation. There is no setting that turns it off, and since
2.1.232 (August 2026) it has been on by default. The anomaly was detected by DRIM in Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export:
grouping claude_code.api_request events by query_source showed agent_summary costing more than the main conversation itself . query_source = agent_summary week before the hook 2 days after share of all Claude Code spend 16.4 % (main conversation: 15.7 %) 0 % share of all API requests 19.7 % , about 1 in 5 0 % part of that spend on Opus 96 % — input tokens per output token ≈ 9,000 : 1 — Spend here means Claude Code's own per-request estimate ( cost_usd ), not an invoice: on a
subscription, what you lose is rate-limit headroom. We are not the only ones who measured it: #86879 collects four independent
measurements of 18–26 %. The fix (how it works) no-agent-summary.js is a Bun preload (~70 lines of code). It wraps only the global setTimeout , the one the summary timer is armed through; when a callback's source text contains
a summarizer anchor (e.g. the [AgentSummary] Timer fired log line), it returns an inert handle instead of arming the timer. Every other timer passes
through untouched. In the OpenTelemetry export the suppressed requests are claude_code.api_request events with query_source = agent_summary . Why a timer hook rather than something simpler: the module ships as precompiled Bun bytecode, so
editing its JS text inside the binary changes nothing, and the API client does not go through a
wrapped globalThis.fetch . But Function.prototype.toString still returns a callback's source
even when it runs from bytecode, so the timer can be recognised by a string inside it. The inert
timer uses exactly 2³¹−1 ms: Node and Bun treat a larger delay as 1 ms, so an "infinite" delay
would fire at once. Which processes it touches The hook installs only inside Claude Code: Bun.main must be /$bunfs/root/cli (the compiled
entry, the same on every row below) and process.execPath must be a Claude Code install. Any other bun , or a compiled Bun binary with another entry name, loads the file and does nothing. install channel (Linux, measured with claude --version ) process.execPath nix …/bin/.claude-wrapped npm @anthropic-ai/claude-code …/@anthropic-ai/claude-code/bin/claude.exe ( .exe on Linux too) npm platform package …/@anthropic-ai/claude-code-linux-x64/claude native installer ~/.local/share/claude/versions/<version> macOS and Windows are not measured; the hook installs there only if they produce these same
shapes, and Verify step 1 tells you. One known pass-through: a foreign binary built with bun build --compile --outfile cli and renamed claude ; there, only timers whose callback
carries an anchor change. Install Put no-agent-summary.js somewhere stable; note its absolute path. Set BUN_OPTIONS globally so every Claude Code process gets it. Write --preload=<path> , with = : BUN_OPTIONS reaches every bun on the machine, and with a
space ( --preload <path> ) bun subcommands break ( bun install → error: Script not found "install" ). Claude Code reads both forms. One of: # ~/.profile, ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc export BUN_OPTIONS= " ${BUN_OPTIONS : + $BUN_OPTIONS } --preload=/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js " # ~/.config/fish/config.fish set -gx BUN_OPTIONS " --preload=/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js " # ~/.config/environment.d/50-no-agent-summary.conf (systemd user env; also reaches # user services and timers; applies when the user manager next starts, usually next login) BUN_OPTIONS =-- preload =/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js Or a wrapper named claude earlier on PATH (the case keeps it idempotent when one Claude
Code process starts another, and also recognises the v2 space form): #! /bin/sh HOOK=/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js case " ${BUN_OPTIONS-} " in * " --preload= $HOOK " * | * " --preload $HOOK " * ) ;; * ) export BUN_OPTIONS= " ${BUN_OPTIONS : + $BUN_OPTIONS } --preload= $HOOK " ;; esac : " ${CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG := ${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR :-/ tmp} / no-agent-summary.log} " export CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG exec /path/to/the/real/claude " $@ " Restart the daemon and every already-running session, then start Claude Code from an
environment that has BUN_OPTIONS : claude daemon stop --any Env variable values effect CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MODE off (default), pass off suppresses the summary timer. pass is the A/B control: loads and logs, arms every timer untouched. Any other value warns on stderr and acts as off . CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG file path, optional Appends preload active mode=… bun=… hooked=global.setTimeout on load, one line per matched timer (first 20), and an exit count. CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MARKER file path, optional Overwritten on load with the preload active … line. Nuances Restart the daemon after install. The daemon, pty host and pre-warmed bg-spare sessions
inherit the environment of the client that started the daemon, so a daemon started before BUN_OPTIONS was set keeps spawning unhooked sessions. Hence claude daemon stop --any . Headless runs need it too: claude -p , cron, CI, editor integrations. Platform: Linux tested by us, macOS (darwin-arm64) reported working by others, Windows untested (see Which processes it touches ). npm --ignore-scripts : bin/claude stays a shell stub and Bun never starts, so the hook
never runs. Upgrading from v2: overwrite the file in place, switch BUN_OPTIONS to the = form and
restart the daemon. If both forms name the same path, bun loads it once. Two different paths
(say an old copy kept beside the new one) both load: a second v3 copy is a no-op, but v2 has no
such guard, so do not leave a v2 path in BUN_OPTIONS . A/B: CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MODE=pass loads the hook but arms every timer; the summaries come back, which shows the off result is the hook's doing. Background processes: daemon, pty host and bg-spare must carry --preload in their environment ( /proc/<pid>/environ on Linux); if not, restart the daemon. Verify (after every update) Preload loads: BUN_OPTIONS= " --preload= $HOME /.local/share/no-agent-summary.js " CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG=/tmp/nas.log claude --version && cat /tmp/nas.log Expect preload active mode=off … . No line: BUN_OPTIONS did not reach the process, or the
path is not absolute. Timer suppressed: with the same BUN_OPTIONS and CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG=/tmp/nas.log , run
a background subagent for a minute or two. The log shows summary timer #1 suppressed (setTimeout, delay=30000) and the agent's panel status stops
updating.

title: Rising rates of colorectal cancer found in nearly all age groups
abstract:
Rising rates of colorectal cancer found in nearly all age groups Colorectal cancer rates are rising across younger and older age groups, according to a study published in NEJM Evidence . Colorectal cancer, the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths overall in the U.S., ranks first in adults younger than 50 years. The new study found that rising incidence now extends beyond younger adults to nearly all age groups, which has implications for the healthcare system as more diagnoses will create a greater demand for treatment and survivorship care. Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH , Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, and her colleagues used the most recent data from the National Cancer Institute to examine incidence rates of colorectal cancer over a 20-year period. The data showed that the age-adjusted incidence rate fell from 55.2 per 100,000 in 2000 to 36.7 in 2022, then rose to 38.3 in 2023. “This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years,” Murphy said, noting that for decades, incidence rates had been declining. This latest study shows that the rates are rising across all age groups up to 65-69. As an epidemiologist studying colorectal cancer trends, she anticipated that a swelling tidal wave of colorectal cancer rates would occur in older populations in addition to those under 50. She describes this phenomenon as the “birth cohort effect,” whereby people born in the 1960s and later face higher risk of colorectal cancer as they reach middle age and older adulthood. “I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time,” Murphy explained. “As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we’re going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed.” The authors saw the sharpest increase in incidence rates among the 45-49-year-old age group, with an increase of 12.76% annually from 2019-2023. They said that this increase is likely driven by more people undergoing colorectal cancer screening after national recommendations lowered the age to begin screening from 50 to 45. “That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do — it’s catching cancer earlier,” Murphy said. However, that does not explain the rise in incidence overall or for other age-specific groups. Increasing rates among those aged 65-69 and plateaus among 70-74-year-olds are concerning as these groups were historically the biggest beneficiaries of screening and are about 80% up-to-date with screening. This suggests unknown risk factors may be offsetting the gains made by screening. The researchers also explored the potential impact of disruptions to screening and diagnoses during the COVID-19 pandemic, but found that even when data from 2020-2021 were excluded, the increase persisted. Screening had largely returned to pre-pandemic levels by January 2021, making COVID unlikely to explain the increase seen in 2023. “These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced,” said Sonia Kupfer, MD , director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine. Not just a problem for young people According to American Cancer Society statistics from 2013-2022, colorectal cancer incidence rates among adults aged 20-49 years increased by 3% annually. This troubling rise in cases of early-onset colorectal cancers among people younger than 50 has received mainstream attention. “There are many unique challenges when you're diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it's important that we shine a spotlight on that problem,” Murphy said. “But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study shows that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well.” Although researchers cannot yet pinpoint which risk factors are driving the trend, Murphy and colleagues are looking into environmental chemical exposures as a possible culprit. With Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, the team will measure thousands of environmental exposures at once in a small blood sample to identify which chemicals warrant further research. They will then work with Kupfer to study the effects of those chemicals on the colon by using organoids, specialized models that can grow colons in a dish. The importance of screening The authors call for continued surveillance as registry data are updated annually. If these trends continue, Murphy warns that the increases in diagnoses across a large, aging population may create a heavy burden on the healthcare system for cancer treatment and survivorship care. Until more is known about the risks factors driving these trends, screening remains the best chance to detect colorectal cancer early and prevent it from becoming deadly. National guidelines recommend that adults at average risk should begin regular screening at age 45 and continue through age 75. For those younger than 45 or older than 75, discussion about screening should be individualized based on family history, symptoms, and other medical problems. Colonoscopies remain the gold standard, but there are now newer options such as blood-based and home-based stool tests that screen for colorectal cancer. “There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated,” Kupfer added. For those younger than 45 without risk factors such as genetics or family history who are not yet eligible for screening, she stressed the importance of paying attention to symptoms — such as blood in the stool, changes in bowel habits or unexplained weight loss — and seeing a doctor. The study, “ Colorectal cancer among U.S. adults, 2000-2023 ,” was supported by funding from the National Institutes of Health and the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research Ablon Scholars Program. Additional authors include Folasade P. May from the University of California Los Angeles, Xin Hu from Emory University in Atlanta, and Samir Gupta from the University of California San Diego. UChicago Medicine and the Biological Sciences Division continue to be at the forefront of cancer care and research. In April 2027, UChicago Medicine will open the AbbVie Foundation Cancer Pavilion , Chicago’s first freestanding cancer pavilion, to bring advanced diagnostics, innovative treatments, translational discoveries, and comprehensive support to patients and the community. AbbVie Foundation Cancer Pavilion As Chicago’s first freestanding cancer pavilion, this 575,000-square-foot facility will provide patients and the community access to the newest diagnostic innovations and leading-edge therapies. Learn about our new cancer pavilion. Sonia Kupfer, MD Sonia Kupfer, MD, is a gastroenterologist and an expert in diagnosing and treating genetic disorders including hereditary gastrointestinal cancer syndromes and celiac disease. She serves as director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic and co-director of the Comprehensive Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic. See Dr. Kupfer's profile

title: Why are good developers so wary of agentic development?
abstract:
Why are good developers so wary of agentic development? Rachel Laycock I'm Rachel Laycock, CTO at Thoughtworks. I'm endlessly curious about how technology is changing the way we build software, lead teams and run businesses. This is where I capture ideas before they're fully formed, challenge my own thinking and occasionally wander off on interesting tangents. 29 October 2026 TL;DR Good developers’ caution about agentic development comes from knowing that built isn’t the same as working in production. I’ve been surprised by how many excellent developers have been hesitant to go all in on coding agents. These are people who usually try new ways of working before anyone else and in many cases invent new tools and practices that support building the application well. So why have we had so much reluctance? The easy (lazy?) answer is that they love writing code, or they’re worried about their jobs. I’m sure that’s true for some people, some of the time. And I know it is true for some of the developers I talk to but I always felt there was something else, another fear hiding behind those obvious ones. When we put together the Technology Radar every six months I try to block out a chunk of time for us to do an open space. In September, a discussion we had on agentic development, which pushed it to its limits, finally helped me see clearly what that fear is. Building it right Thoughtworkers care deeply about building the right thing and building it right . It’s pretty much our default way of working and thinking and it’s where many of the practices and technologies we invented and championed came from. We want software that is useful and helpful, can be changed next year, and doesn’t fall over in production. Our developers adopted, championed or invented some of the first versions of continuous integration, pairing, automated testing, continuous delivery, microservices and many others early because they helped us build the software right. Early coding agents made it very easy to produce code, including code we wouldn’t have wanted anywhere near production, written by people who have not learned about the chasm between building something and making it run in production safely. The tools have improved enormously, but experienced developers still have questions. Are we confident this is the right behaviour? Does it work as expected? Are these the right boundaries? Will we be able to evolve it? Does it abide by the principles and practices we learned the hard way to give us confidence it will meet the needs of the customer and stay up in production? What happens when something fails? Will another team be able to live with it? And so on. Underneath all of those sits a bigger question. How much can we trust a system when nobody has experience of building it this way? Let me state that another way. Nearly every system we have in production now was built the old way, by hand, by people we could trust (hopefully). Everything we build now is the new way and we have not lived with that yet. After more than 25 years in technology, I’ve come to value the judgment people develop through experience. I regularly put similar questions to models and to senior technologists at Thoughtworks. For the difficult questions, I still get more useful answers from the humans or maybe more insightful with very specific experience that helps me better understand the point. They challenge the premise, recognise a pattern from something that went wrong ten years ago, or spot the organisational problem hiding inside the technical one. I can now access an extraordinary amount of information. I still need people who can help me think through what matters, I still need wisdom and insight. That type judgment is exactly what hesitant experienced developers are trying to protect. And I want to be clear: they are not hesitant to use a coding assistant, they are hesitant to go all in and let the agents do all the execution. They are hesitant to take their hand off the wheel because they don’t have full confidence the agents have the right guardrails in place to run off on their own. A week at the whiteboard Recently, Giles Alexander, our Regional CTO for Europe, brought senior engineers, infrastructure consultants and product people together for a week of working in exactly this way. No code written by anyone. Everything built by agents. The point wasn’t to prove that an airline application could be built in a week. (Funnily enough they got 80% done and we all know what that means… you can’t make stuff up!) The purpose of the experiment was to learn what happens to the team’s work when agents do all of the coding. You can read some of what they learned here . What struck me in our conversations was how much time they spent at the whiteboard. Working out the domain. Drawing boundaries. Deciding what should happen next and making plans the agents could act on. Meanwhile, the agents kept producing code beyond the team’s working day. The humans were also designing the feedback around that work: tests, contracts, architecture checks and a delivery pipeline. They were working out how to give agents enough freedom to make progress while keeping confidence in the result. Most of the work at the keyboard was directing agents to put this learning into the harness, so the building and testing agents got it right on the next run and they could have more confidence in what they built. Interestingly in the end the product person committed more feature code than anyone else on the team. When I asked them to estimate they said they spend about ⅔ of their time at the whiteboard and ⅓ on the harness, which could give us some clue as to how developers will work in the future, but before you get ahead of yourself redesigning your team, that’s not the end of the story… The application ran. The build was red. The application ran, but the build was frequently red. It worked on their machine - again you couldn’t make this up if you tried! A constant red build gives me the ick. A red build should mean something: stop, investigate, fix it. If it’s red so often that people stop paying attention, how do we spot the next real failure? And if we can’t trust the checks, a green build stops being reassuring too. That’s exactly the uncertainty continuous integration was supposed to remove, and we’ve been advocating it for over 25 years. We’re still working through how to address it. Remember this was an experiment to push the very edge of agentic development. Were too many agents working in parallel and stepping on each other’s changes? Was the system not yet modular enough for agents to work on separate parts? Or were changes simply arriving faster than the checks could finish? Or was it a combination of all of these and more? Either way we definitely need to rethink how we will solve the last mile challenges. I can see continuous delivery/DevOps as a movement having a resurgence and a rethink in the agentic era in the same way the rest of the development life cycle is being upended. And it isn’t just our experiment. DORA’s 2025 research found AI adoption is now linked to higher delivery throughput, but to lower delivery stability. Exactly what continuous delivery and DevOps were trying to solve for! All of these challenges prompted some good arguments internally. What role should test-driven development play when you aren’t reading every line and the agent created the tests alongside the code? Where would acceptance tests, contract tests and checks at system boundaries give us more confidence without being too brittle? How much design should we do before setting an agent loose, given how quickly we can revise an approach? Is there an appropriate point we will know we have gone too far? One of the biggest puzzles in all this is the size of the batch. I have heard many teams are moving from Stories to Epics. Great for speed of development but can your CI pipeline handle that size unit of work at speed and in parallel?

title: Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers–Including Undercover ICE Agents
abstract:
Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story An unprecedented leak of Department of Homeland Security records has exposed details of more than 41,000 employees or contractors who work for the department and its constituent agencies. The records include email addresses, phone numbers, and office addresses, but also references to internal systems and sensitive information on undercover and surveillance programs. In all, the leak provides a map of how DHS is organized and how it operates. The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. DDoSecrets published the archive, which it calls “Icepick,” on Wednesday. In a press release, DDoSecrets says the data is from DHS's Okta login system. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. “We are aware of this report. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” the spokesperson says. The leak comes as DHS has aggressively pursued its critics , seeking to unmask anonymous social media users, obtain customer records on protesters, and secure warrants for surveillance tools aimed at reporters. Since the start of the second Trump administration, DHS and the federal government have moved to hide DHS employees’ names and faces . The agency has also expanded its definition of “doxing”—a term that typically refers to publishing someone’s home address and other personal details for malicious purposes—to encompass the publication of basic facts about public employees, like their names and titles. The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families. Law enforcement agencies have arrested several suspects and detained another who is alleged to be part of the group. The DHS records are searchable on a website crimew built. “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them,” she tells WIRED. “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively,” a Homeland Security spokesperson tells WIRED. “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” The DOJ did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. The FBI referred WIRED’s inquiry to DHS. According to a WIRED analysis of the data, CBP staffers account for more than half of the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing. Another 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more than half of them contractors. Altogether, the files cover about a seventh of DHS’s workforce, revealing how DHS is structured, from senior leadership down to individual immigration agents and detention contractors. Like most large organizations, DHS uses permission groups to control access to internal systems, according to the leaked records. Nearly everyone named in the leak has access to at least some of these systems. At HSI, 39 employees across more than a dozen field offices belong to groups whose names include “CUC,” which government court filings say stands for “certified undercover operation.” Another group, apparently based in HSI's St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations, references "Keyhole," which federal court filings describe as a certified undercover operation that recently funded HSI’s undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups earlier this year. Others reference a “Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).” The names of the groups—there are over 55,000 in all—appear to reference tools for accessing immigration court records, pulling data from seized phones, and conducting surveillance. These include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media. Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS's web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who has returned to defense tech company Anduril ; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. One, called “Grok.com,” includes eight DHS technology officials, including the department’s former chief information officer and chief data officer. “If authentic and current, this is an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS,” says Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at the threat intelligence company Recorded Future. “This dataset becomes way more valuable when correlated with previously compromised information, commercial data, and other intelligence collections. An adversary could spend months exploiting these relationships to identify vulnerable personnel, develop convincing impersonation attempts, or compromise ongoing investigations.” More than 700 accounts are associated with a group apparently referencing Signal , the encrypted messaging app, nearly all belonging to CBP personnel. More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencing Mobile Fortify , a face-recognition app that immigration agents use to identify people. The group includes field supervisors, special response team operators, and tactical and intelligence agents. About half are in Texas, California, and Arizona. Roughly 1,300 ICE enforcement accounts have been created since July 4, 2025, when Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which funded the hiring of 10,000 new ICE Enforcement and Removal officers by the end of 2025. Nearly 20 accounts appear to belong to personnel with the Department of Defense, which the administration styles as the Department of War; eight are in a group titled “ICE Tip Line DOW Surge.” About 170 accounts are listed as providing “military processing support” at ICE facilities, and 35 others explicitly identify National Guard members. Dozens of accounts have job titles like “Designated Immigration Officer” and “287(g) Officer,” which mark local law enforcement personnel authorized to carry out some immigration enforcement duties . Many list county sheriff's offices and jails as their workplaces. The records also include roughly 4,400 “associates,” whose jobs range from IT developers and data scientists to nurses and detention officers. Of those, 145 are named as a “contractor” or “high risk contractor.” More than 300 records reference senior titles associated with DHS headquarters, from Noem down through deputy undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, and chiefs of staff to officials overseeing intelligence, technology, biometrics, and privacy.

title: H.264 Is Magic (2016)
abstract:
H.264 is a video compression codec standard. It is ubiquitous - internet video, Blu-ray, phones, security cameras, drones, everything. Everything uses H.264 now. H.264 is a remarkable piece of technology. It is the result of 30+ years of work with one single goal: To reduce the bandwidth required for transmission of full-motion video. Technically, it is very interesting. This post will give insight into some of the details at a high level - I hope to not bore you too much with the intricacies. Also note that many of the concepts explained here apply to video compression in general, and not just H.264. Why even compress anything? A simple uncompressed video file will contain an array of 2D buffers containing pixel data for each frame. So it's a 3D (2 spatial dimensions and 1 temporal) array of bytes. Each pixel takes 3 bytes to store - one byte each for the three primary colors (red, green and blue). 1080p @ 60 Hz = 1920x1080x60x3 => ~ 370 MB/sec of raw data. This is next to impossible to deal with. A 50GB Blu-ray disk will only hold ~2 mins. You can't move it anywhere fast. Even SSDs have trouble dumping this straight from RAM to Disk[^1]. So yeah. We need compression. Why H.264 compression? Yes, I will answer this. But first let me show you something. Here is the Apple Homepage: I captured the screen of this home page and produced two files: PNG screenshot of the Apple homepage 1015KB 5 Second 60fps H.264 video of the same Apple homepage 175KB Eh. What? Those file sizes look switched. No, they're right. The H.264 video, 300 frames long is 175KB. A single frame of that video in PNG is 1015KB. It looks like we're storing 300 times the amount of data in the video. But the file size is a fifth. So H.264 would seem to be 1500x as efficient as PNG. How is this even possible? All right, what's the trick? There are very many tricks! H.264 uses all the tricks you can think of (and tons you can't think of). Let's go through the important ones. Shedding weight Imagine you're building a car for street racing. You need to go faster. What is the first thing you do? You shed some weight. Your car weighs 3000 lbs. You throw away stuff you don't need. Those back seats? pfft. Chuck those. That subwoofer? Gone. No music for you. Air Conditioning? Yeah, ditch it. Transmission? Ye..no. Wait! We're gonna need that. You remove everything except the things that matter. This concept of throwing away bits you don't need to save space is called lossy compression. H.264 is a lossy codec - it throws away less important bits and only keeps the important bits. PNG is a lossless codec. It means that nothing is thrown away. Bit for bit, the original source image can be recovered from a PNG encoded image. Important bits? How does the algorithm know what bits in my frame are important? There are few obvious ways to trim out images. Maybe the top right quadrant is useless all the time. So maybe we can zero out those pixels and discard that quadrant. We would use only 3/4th of the space we need. ~2200 lbs now. Or maybe we can crop out a thick border around the edges of the frame, the important stuff is in the middle anyway. Yes, you could do these. But H.264 doesn't do this. What does H.264 actually do? H.264, like other lossy image algorithms, discards detail information. Here is a close-up of the original compared with the image post-discard. See how the compressed one does not show the holes in the speaker grills in the MacBook Pro? If you don't zoom in, you would even notice the difference. The image on the right weighs in at 7% the size of the original - and we haven't even compressed the image in the traditional sense. Imagine your car weighed just 200 lbs! 7% wow! How do you discard detail information like that? For this we need a quick math lesson. Information Entropy Now we're getting to the juicy bits! Ha puns! If you took an information theory class, you might remember information entropy. Information entropy is the number of bits required to represent some information. Note that it is not simply the size of some dataset. It is minimum number of bits that must be used to represent all the information contained in a dataset. For example, if your dataset is the result of a single coin toss, you need 1 bit of entropy. If you have record two coin tosses, you'll need 2 bits. Makes sense? Suppose you have some strange coin - you've tossed it 10 times, and every time it lands on heads. How would you describe this information to someone? You wouldn't say HHHHHHHHH. You would just say "10 tosses, all heads" - bam! You've just compressed some data! Easy. I saved you hours of mindfuck lectures. This is obviously an oversimplification, but you've transformed some data into another shorter representation of the same information. You've reduced data redundancy . The information entropy in this dataset has not changed - you've just converted between representations. This type of encoder is called an entropy encoder - it's a general-purpose lossless encoder that works for any type of data. Frequency Domain Now that you understand information entropy, let's move on to transformations of data. You can represent data in some fundamental units. If you use binary, you have 0 and 1. If you use hex, you have 16 characters. You can easily transform between the two systems. They are essentially equivalent. So far so good? Ok! Now, some imagination! Imagine you can transform any dataset that varies over space(or time) - something like the brightness value of an image, into a different coordinate space. So instead of x-y coordinates, let's say we have frequency coordinates. freqX and freqY are the axes now. This is called a frequency domain representation. There is another mindfuck mathematical theorem[^2] that states that you can do this for any data and you can achieve a perfect lossless transformation as long as freqX and freqY are high enough. Okay, but what the freq are freqX and freqY? freqX and freqY are some other set of basis units. Just like when we switch from binary to hex, we have a different fundamental unit, we're switching from the familiar X-Y to freqX and freqY. Hex 'A' looks different from binary '1010'. Both mean the same thing, but look different. So here is what our image looks like in the frequency domain: The fine grill on that MacBook pro has a high information content in the higher frequency components of that image. Finely varying content = high frequency components. Any sort of gradual variation in the color and brightness - such as gradients are low frequency components of that image. Anything in between falls in between. So fine details = high freq. Gentle gradients = low freq. Makes sense? In the frequency domain representation, the low frequency components are near the center of that image. The higher frequency components are towards of the edges of the image. Okay. Kinda makes sense. But why do all this? Because now, you can take that frequency domain image and then mask out the edges - discard information which will contain the information with high frequency components. Now if you convert back to your regular x-y coordinates, you'll find that the resulting image looks similar to the original but has lost some of the fine details. But now, the image only occupies a fraction of the space. By controlling how big your mask is, you can now tune precisely how detailed you want your output images to be. Here is the close-up of the laptop in the home page again. Except now, there is a circular border mask that's been applied. The numbers represent the information entropy of that image as a fraction of the original. Even at 2%, you won't notice the difference unless you're at this zoom level. 2%! - your car now weighs 60 lbs! So that's how you shed weight. This process in lossy compression is called quantization [^3]. Okay. Impressive, I guess. What else you got? Chroma Subsampling. The human/eye brain system is not very good at resolving finer details in color.

title: Gemini 4 Carbon
abstract:
Gemini 4 Carbon: our next frontier model Oct 28, 2026 | Gemini 4 Carbon is our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Koray Kavukcuoglu SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates. Building on Gemini 4 Argon , which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem. We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program . We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible. Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price 1 as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price. Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasks Designed to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems. Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena . State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems Gemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative. Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails): Finding real vulnerabilities: Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro , autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software. Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. Carbon sets a new state-of-the-art on the popular exploitation benchmark ExploitGym (54.8%). Patching at the root cause: Ultimately after identifying the vulnerabilities, fixing the root cause is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench , turning validated findings directly into working code fixes. Advancing frontier model safety & security Gemini 4 Carbon builds on the same multi-layered safety and security stack of Argon — combining model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring. In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our Safety and Security report . With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way. Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation: With Carbon, we further mitigated shortcut attempts in training while ensuring high-quality coding performance. Carbon reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0.0%, with attempts to cheat dropping to 0.4% — all while improving overall accuracy. In live coding environments with our internal teams, we observed that high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%. Greater transparency and honesty: In our internal testing, Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon. It puts methodological caveats directly into the deliverable or withholds blocked actions with a clear list of what remains required, rather than fabricating or hedging around missing evidence. Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity: Rather than guessing or forcing a path forward, Carbon retrieves the relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting — as a result, users should observe a much better collaborative experience with Carbon. Following through without overstepping: Carbon simultaneously reduced overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% resulting in much more reliable execution of multi-step plans end-to-end while respecting project constraints and staying strictly within scope. Resisting prompt injection: While Argon previously led the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark in prompt injection resistance with a very low 0.7% attack success rate, Carbon achieves 0.0% — resisting every evaluated attack attempt. Coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumers Pushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment. With Gemini 4 Carbon, our goal is to deliver meaningful leaps in software engineering and cybersecurity defense without compromising on safety or reliability. We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon. Posted in:

title: Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5
abstract:
Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 See model page Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, and second only to Claude Opus 5.5 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index Gemini 4 Carbon scores 59 on Intelligence Index v5, driven by leading performance in complex reasoning, knowledge, and scientific tasks. It also has large gains in coding and knowledge work, particularly when compared to other Gemini models, but it is not leading in all these areas. As with launch of Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 4 Carbon is being rolled out to selected users and is not yet publicly available. Google is offering a 50% launch discount, with no confirmed end date. All our charts and figures use standard pricing for both Gemini 4 Carbon and Argon. Key results for Gemini 4 Carbon with high reasoning: ➤ Gemini 4 Carbon leads the Intelligence Index v5, with the #1 score in 4 of the 9 Index evaluations: HLE-Diamond, Terminal-Bench-Science, AA-Omniscience, AutomationBench-AA. Carbon makes substantial gains elsewhere but is not leading in coding and knowledge work ➤ Behind only Claude Opus 5.5 on coding agents: With Antigravity CLI, Gemini 4 Carbon (high) scores 59 only 3 points behind Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 62) on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index. Carbon ranks second on both Terminal-Bench 4.0 (64%) and FrontierCode v1.1 (51%), behind Claude Opus 5.5 (max) at 56%. Google has historically underperformed in this area and so this improvement stands out. ➤ Improved agentic knowledge work, but not yet leading: On AA-Briefcase, Gemini 4 Carbon (high) scores 1609 Elo, a 126-point improvement over Gemini 4 Argon (high, 1483), but still behind models including Grok 4.7 (xhigh, 1638), Muse Wonder (max, 1659) and Kimi K3.1 Pro (1678). The largest gain comes from Presentation, up 293 Elo to 1598, alongside a 120-point improvement in Analytical Quality to 1671 ➤ Lower Cost per Task than Claude Opus 5.5 for comparable overall intelligence: With standard pricing, Gemini 4 Carbon costs $7.76 per Intelligence Index task, ~23% less than Claude Opus 5.5 (max, $10.04) but ~1.2x GPT-6 Astra (max, $6.25). It uses 123k output tokens per task, 29% fewer than Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 173k). At the same $4/$20 standard pricing, its Cost per Task is in line with Gemini 4 Argon ($7.68), while scoring 9 points higher on the Intelligence Index ➤ Leading AA-Omniscience v1.1 score, with low hallucination: Gemini 4 Carbon scores 54 on our recently updated AA-Omniscience v1.1, 6 points ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 48) and 8 points ahead of Gemini 4 Argon (46). Accuracy (% correct) rises 10 points over Argon to 58%, while its hallucination rate rises from 4% to 11%. This is still the second lowest of any model, behind only Argon, compared with 50% for both Claude Opus 5.5 (max) and GPT-6 Astra (max) Key model details: ➤ Context Window: 1M tokens ➤ Multimodality: Text, image, video, and speech input, with text output ➤ Pricing: $4/$20 per 1M input/output tokens, the same as Gemini 4 Argon’s standard pricing, with a 50% discount. Cached input tokens receive a 95% discount ($0.20 per 1M at standard pricing)

title: Improving dysarthric speech classification with generative AI-based data augmentation.
abstract: Dysarthria is a neurological speech disorder characterized by impaired motor control of speech production, resulting in reduced intelligibility. It commonly arises in the context of neurodegenerative conditions, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and cerebral palsy. The development of deep learning systems for dysarthria assessment is hindered by the scarcity of annotated data, which restricts the ability of models to generalize to unseen speakers. This study proposes a cross-corpus diffusion-based data augmentation strategy for improving automatic speech intelligibility classification from dysarthric speech. A Grad-TTS model is trained on dysarthric speakers from the TORGO dataset and used to synthesize the vocabulary of UA-Speech, producing speaker-conditioned samples intended to transfer pathological acoustic traits across corpora. The proposed strategy is evaluated both independently and in combination with conventional signal-level augmentation using ResNet-50 and ResNet-152 classifiers in binary and four-class intelligibility classification tasks. The results indicate that cross-corpus synthetic augmentation improves average performance and that, in most settings, its integration with conventional augmentation yields further gains, suggesting that the two strategies introduce complementary forms of variability.
